bugs.title: normalize_features always re-fits the scaler, leaking test statistics (the passed-in scaler is ignored)
bugs.description: normalize_features unconditionally calls scaler.fit_transform(X) at line 227. The only effect of passing scaler=<fitted scaler> is to skip constructing a fresh StandardScaler; the fit is then re-run on whatever X is given. So when load_split_data does `X_test, _ = normalize_features(X_test, scaler=scaler)` (line 379) — and identically in pred_pos_lstm_one_prediction.py:799 and pred_pos_lstm_many_predictions.py:521 — the test set is normalized with the TEST set's own mean/std, not the training statistics.
bugs.why_wrong: Correct preprocessing fits the scaler on train only and applies (transform, not fit_transform) the frozen train statistics to test/inference data. Here both train and test get fit_transform, so (a) it is data leakage / an invalid evaluation (test is standardized to its own distribution), and (b) at deployment/inference on a single new trajectory the input is normalized by that trajectory's own stats, which differs from training-time normalization and silently degrades or invalidates predictions. The docstring/comment 'use the same scaler for test data' is contradicted by the code.
bugs.fix_sketch: Branch on whether the scaler was supplied: `if scaler is None: scaler = StandardScaler(); X_normalized = scaler.fit_transform(X) else: X_normalized = scaler.transform(X)`. Then load_split_data's intent (fit on train, transform test) actually holds, and inference uses the persisted train scaler.

bugs.title: load_much_data train branch reads `start` that is only assigned in the test branch
bugs.description: `start` is assigned only inside `if dir in test_dir:` (line 180). The training branch (`elif dir in train_dirs:`) uses `start` at lines 198 and 203 (`new_data_dict[key][start:start+N_points_per_dir]`). It does not NameError only because `dirs` is sorted and test_dir = dirs[:1], so the test directory is always iterated first and leaves `start` bound. The training slice therefore inherits the TEST directory's offset value — including its random offset when random_start=True (line 180 sets start to np.random.randint(0,20000)).
bugs.why_wrong: This is an implicit cross-branch dependency on iteration order and a semantic bug: the training data's start offset is taken from the test recording, not chosen for the training recording. If the directory ordering ever changed, or test_dir were processed after a train dir, it would raise NameError. With random_start the train windows start at a test-derived random index for the FIRST train dir's first-assignment path; combined with the vstack inconsistency below, behavior is incoherent.
bugs.fix_sketch: Define `start` independently per directory (or per branch) before slicing in each branch, e.g. compute a train-specific start (0 or its own random offset, bounds-checked against that dir's length) inside the train branch.

bugs.title: Inconsistent slicing: first-assignment uses start:start+N, vstack path uses :N (drops the offset)
bugs.description: For both X-test/y-test and X-train/y-train, the first time a key is populated the code slices `new_data_dict[key][start:start+N]` (lines 185,190,198,203), but every subsequent directory's vstack uses `new_data_dict[key][:N]` (lines 187,192,200,205), ignoring `start` entirely.
bugs.why_wrong: The windowing offset is applied to the first directory only and silently dropped for all others. With random_start this means directory 1 is sampled from a random position while directories 2..n are always sampled from index 0 — an inconsistent sampling scheme. It also means the random_start bounds check at line 181 (which can reset start to 0) only ever guards the first directory.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use the same `start:start+N` slice in both the first-assignment and vstack branches (and recompute a valid, bounds-checked start per directory).

bugs.title: Off-by-one: train_dirs[:n_dirs_to_use+1] selects one extra directory
bugs.description: train_dirs is first set to dirs[1:num_datasets+1] (line 133), then truncated to train_dirs[:n_dirs_to_use+1] (line 141). The `+1` makes it keep n_dirs_to_use+1 directories. Combined with N_points = N_points_per_dir * len(train_dirs) (line 143) and the per-dir accumulation `Nloaded_points += N_points_per_dir` with `if Nloaded_points >= N_points: break` (lines 194,206-207), the count of points actually loaded and the requested N_train can diverge.
bugs.why_wrong: n_dirs_to_use = max(1, int(N_train/N_points_per_dir)) is already the number of directories needed to reach N_train points; slicing with +1 keeps an extra directory. The total N_points is then computed from the (over-long) train_dirs length, so the loaded training-set size is generally not N_train and depends on rounding interactions between N_points_per_dir (floored to a multiple of seq_length) and the dir count. The print at line 145 ('Loading a total of {N_train}...') is therefore misleading.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use train_dirs[:n_dirs_to_use] (no +1) and derive N_points from min(num_datasets, n_dirs_to_use); reconcile the floor/modulo math so requested vs loaded point counts match, or document the intended approximation.

bugs.title: create_sequences `overlap` semantic is inverted/confusing; defaults disagree across the codebase
bugs.description: Stride is `seq_length - overlap` (line 102). So `overlap` is actually the number of overlapping samples, but the default is overlap=1, giving stride seq_length-1 (windows shifted by one sample => ~99% overlap, max redundancy). Meanwhile load_split_data passes overlap=0 by default (params at line 256), giving stride=seq_length (non-overlapping/tiling). The name suggests a fraction or a boolean to many callers.
bugs.why_wrong: The parameter named 'overlap' does not mean fraction of overlap nor a stride; it is (seq_length - stride). overlap=0 => no overlap, overlap=1 => maximum overlap — the opposite of the intuitive reading. If overlap >= seq_length, stride <= 0 and range() yields no iterations (silent empty output). The mismatch between the function default (1) and the load_split_data default (0) means calling create_sequences directly vs through load_split_data produces drastically different window counts and overlap, affecting both train redundancy and how trajectory reconstruction (cumsum of per-window deltas) lines up.
bugs.fix_sketch: Rename to `stride` (samples to advance) or make `overlap` a clearly-documented count with validation (0 <= overlap < seq_length, else raise). Make the default consistent with load_split_data, and assert stride > 0.

bugs.title: calculate_position_difference mutates its input array in place
bugs.description: The loop does `y[i] -= y[i][0]` (line 403) on the passed-in array and returns the same object. Because y is a NumPy array (and y[i] is a view), this subtracts each window's first row from the window in place, mutating the caller's array.
bugs.why_wrong: An in-place mutation through a returned-and-reassigned variable is a footgun: if the caller still holds a reference to the original y (e.g. ground-truth positions reused for plotting/metrics, or the same array sliced into train and test), those references are silently corrupted with relative coordinates. It also makes the function non-idempotent. The 'difference relative to window start' transform should produce a new array.
bugs.fix_sketch: Return `y - y[:, 0:1, :]` (vectorized, allocates a new array) or `y_out = y.copy(); y_out -= y_out[:, [0]]; return y_out`. Avoid mutating the argument.

bugs.title: Sequences are built across concatenated multi-trajectory / train+test data with no per-recording boundaries
bugs.description: load_much_data vstacks data from multiple directories into single X-train/X-test arrays (lines 187-205), then load_split_data hstacks features and calls create_sequences once over the whole concatenated array (lines 382-388). create_sequences has no notion of recording boundaries, so a window can span the seam between two different recordings.
bugs.why_wrong: For inertial navigation, a window must come from one continuous trajectory: orientation, world-frame rotation, and double-integration of acceleration are only meaningful within a single contiguous recording with a consistent clock and initial pose. A window straddling the boundary between recording A's tail and recording B's head produces a physically meaningless input/target (discontinuous position, time, and orientation), and for the position-delta targets (last-minus-first within window) the delta crosses two unrelated coordinate origins. The number of corrupted windows equals roughly (num_dirs - 1) per split.
bugs.fix_sketch: Run create_sequences per directory/trajectory and concatenate the resulting window tensors, never tile across the concatenation seam; carry per-window provenance so reconstruction (cumsum of deltas) restarts at each trajectory's true initial position.

bugs.title: random_start bounds check uses an arbitrary 20000 cap and only checks the first feature's length
bugs.description: start is drawn from np.random.randint(0, 20000) (hardcoded), and the overflow guard at line 181 checks only `new_data_dict[list(new_data_dict.keys())[0]]` length and resets to 0 if start+N_test exceeds it.
bugs.why_wrong: 20000 is a magic number unrelated to actual recording length; a recording shorter than 20000 samples will frequently trigger the reset-to-0 path (so 'random' start collapses to deterministic 0 for short files), and a recording longer than 20000 never samples its tail. The length check assumes all features share the same length as keys()[0]; if synced/raw streams have different lengths the slice can silently under/over-read other features.
bugs.fix_sketch: Derive the upper bound from the actual usable length (len(stream) - N) and validate that all selected feature streams have equal length before slicing.

bugs.title: split_data is defined but the train/test split is actually done by directory in load_much_data; split_data is unused dead code with a non-shuffled cut
bugs.description: split_data does a positional cut (first 80% train, last 20% test) over already-windowed data with no shuffling, and is not used by load_split_data (which splits by directory instead). It is imported nowhere in the call sites surveyed.
bugs.why_wrong: If it were used, a positional cut on overlapping windows would leak: adjacent train/test windows share samples (with overlap>0 the train tail and test head overlap heavily), and a contiguous time split on one trajectory puts correlated neighboring windows on both sides. As written it is dead code that can mislead future maintainers into a leaky split.
bugs.fix_sketch: Either remove it, or if retained, split before windowing on contiguous trajectory blocks with a guard gap >= seq_length between train and test to prevent window overlap leakage.

bugs.title: include_clusters mutates the caller's columns_X list (appends 'cluster_labels')
bugs.description: When include_clusters is True, columns_X.append('cluster_labels') (line 148) mutates the list passed by the caller (params['input'] from load_split_data). Similarly params['input'].append('theta') at line 351 mutates the shared params dict's list.
bugs.why_wrong: Mutating an input list as a side effect means repeated calls (e.g. in a hyperparameter loop reusing the same params dict) accumulate duplicate 'cluster_labels'/'theta' entries, which then break col_locations width accounting and hstack ordering on the second iteration onward.
bugs.fix_sketch: Operate on a local copy: `columns_X = list(columns_X) + ['cluster_labels']`; likewise build a local input list rather than appending to params['input'].

bugs.title: Module-level Theta divides sin term by |w|·dt/2 instead of |w| (wrong by factor 2/dt = 400 at 200 Hz)
bugs.description: Theta computes `np.cos(u_b_norm/2)*np.eye(4) + np.sin(u_b_norm/2)/(u_b_norm/2)*W`, where u_b_norm = |u| = |w|·dt and W = Omega(w) is the FULL (non-halved) 4x4 skew. The coefficient on W is therefore sin(|w|dt/2)/(|w|dt/2).
bugs.why_wrong: The correct discrete propagator q_{k+1}=exp(0.5·Omega_full·dt)·q_k = cos(|w|dt/2)·I + (sin(|w|dt/2)/|w|)·Omega_full(w)·q_k. The coefficient on Omega_full must be sin(|w|dt/2)/|w|, NOT sin(|w|dt/2)/(|w|dt/2). The code's denominator is |w|dt/2 instead of |w|, i.e. divided by an extra dt/2, so the rotation (off-diagonal) part is scaled by 2/dt. At dt=1/200 that is a factor of 400 too large — I verified numerically that Theta_mod[0,1]/Theta_correct[0,1] == 399.9999... The matrix is no longer even approximately a unit-quaternion update; propagating with it explodes the off-diagonal and the per-step renormalization in the caller cannot recover the correct rotation. (Note u_b_norm/2 ≈ sin(u_b_norm/2) only for tiny angles, which is why the diagonal looks fine, but the off-diagonal scaling is catastrophically wrong.)
bugs.fix_sketch: Use the rotation-vector magnitude as the denominator and the half-angle = |w|·dt/2 inside the trig: `ang = vec_norm(w)*dt; return np.cos(ang/2)*np.eye(4) + (np.sin(ang/2)/vec_norm(w))*W` with W = full skew. Equivalently keep dividing by u_b_norm but multiply by dt: `np.sin(u_b_norm/2)/u_b_norm * W`. Add a small-angle / |w|≈0 guard returning np.eye(4).

bugs.title: Inner Theta (in load_split_data) rotates at HALF the true rate (halved Omega but |w| denominator)
bugs.description: The Omega defined inside load_split_data multiplies the whole 4x4 skew by `.5` (line 293), and the inner Theta (line 334) is `np.cos(u_b_norm/2)*np.eye(4) + (np.sin(u_b_norm/2)/w_norm)*W` where w_norm = |w| (correct denominator) and W is the HALVED Omega.
bugs.why_wrong: With the correct |w| denominator the multiplier on the skew must be applied to the FULL skew (Omega_full). Because this inner Omega is pre-multiplied by 0.5, the off-diagonal/rotation term is exactly half of the correct value — I verified Theta_inner[0,1]/Theta_correct[0,1] == 0.5 exactly. So the `theta` feature fed to the model encodes orientation increments at half the real angular rate. This is a different bug from the module-level Theta (that one is 400x too large; this one is 2x too small), and they coexist — two definitions, two distinct errors. This Theta is the one actually used to build the `data['X-train']['theta']` / `X-test` feature (lines 336-349), so the trained model ingests systematically half-rate orientation increments.
bugs.fix_sketch: Either drop the `*.5` on the inner Omega (line 293) so W is the full skew, OR halve the denominator (divide sin by w_norm/2). Pick one; do not do both. Then this matches the corrected module-level form.

bugs.title: Two inconsistent Omega definitions (factor-of-2 difference between module-level and inner)
bugs.description: Inner Omega (285-293) returns the 4x4 skew multiplied by 0.5; module-level Omega (423-436) returns the same skew with NO 0.5 factor. I confirmed numerically that Omega_module(w) == 2 * Omega_inner(w) elementwise, and both share the same sign convention and scalar-LAST [x,y,z,w] layout.
bugs.why_wrong: The continuous kinematics are qdot = 0.5·Omega_full·q, so the 0.5 belongs in the propagator/exponent, not baked into Omega. Having two Omega definitions that differ by 2x means the two Theta callers behave differently and any future caller cannot know which convention applies. The standard form keeps Omega = full skew and puts 0.5 in qdot/exp; the inner version's baked-in 0.5 is the proximate cause of the half-rate bug above.
bugs.fix_sketch: Delete the inner duplicate definitions of Omega/u_b/Theta entirely and import/use the module-level ones; standardize on Omega = full (non-halved) skew with 0.5 only inside the exponential. Remove the redundant module-level u_b/is_column_vector if folding into one definition.

bugs.title: Quaternion convention mismatch: r2q/q2r are scalar-FIRST [w,x,y,z] but Omega/Theta are scalar-LAST [x,y,z,w]
bugs.description: rotation_matrix_2_quaternion writes q[0]=sqrt(1+trace)/2 (the scalar) and q[1..3] the vector part — scalar-first [w,x,y,z]; quat_2_rotation_matrix likewise treats q[0] as the scalar (verified: q2r(r2q(R))==R exactly under scalar-first). But Omega places the gyro 3-vector `w` in the 4th row/column, so Omega/Theta act on a scalar-LAST [x,y,z,w] quaternion.
bugs.why_wrong: In get_orientations (transformer_informed.py:97-106) the initial orientation is built with rotation_matrix_2_quaternion -> scalar-FIRST, then propagated as `Theta(...) @ orientations[seq,i-1]` (line 111) -> scalar-LAST operator. The scalar component (real part) is in slot 0 of the seed but slot 3 of the operator, so the propagation rotates the wrong components and treats the real part as a vector axis. The result is a meaningless quaternion stream even if Theta itself were correct. Reader/writer of the orientation representation disagree on layout.
bugs.fix_sketch: Pick one convention repo-wide (scalar-last [x,y,z,w] is conventional for this Omega). Rewrite rotation_matrix_2_quaternion / quat_2_rotation_matrix to put the scalar in slot 3, or reorder the seed quaternion before feeding it to Theta. Add an assertion/test that q2r(propagate(seed)) stays orthonormal.

bugs.title: rotation_matrix_2_quaternion divides by 4*q0 with no guard against q0->0 (180deg) singularity
bugs.description: q[0]=sqrt(1+R00+R11+R22)/2, then q[1..3] = (off-diagonal diff)/(4*q[0]). When the rotation is near 180deg the trace -> -1, so 1+R00+R11+R22 -> 0, q0 -> 0, and the three divisions blow up (inf/NaN). For trace < -1 from numerical error, the sqrt also takes a negative argument and returns NaN.
bugs.why_wrong: A correct rotation->quaternion conversion must select the largest-magnitude component (Shepperd's / branchless method) to avoid division by a near-zero scalar, and clamp the sqrt argument to >=0. This single-branch formula is only safe when q0 is comfortably nonzero. Phone orientations routinely pass through configurations where the body-to-world matrix has trace near -1, producing NaN seeds that then poison the whole propagated sequence.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use the 4-case Shepperd method (compute from whichever of 1±R00±R11±R22 is largest) or scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.from_matrix(R).as_quat(); clamp sqrt args with np.maximum(0,...). Normalize the result.

bugs.title: get_body2world_rot DOWN axis = +accelerometer, but specific force points UP (sign flip)
bugs.description: DOWN = a0 (the raw accelerometer reading), normalized. The trailing comment `# maybe a minus sign is needed` flags the authors' own uncertainty.
bugs.why_wrong: A stationary accelerometer measures specific force, which points UP (the reaction to gravity), magnitude ~9.8. So a0 points opposite to physical down. Setting DOWN=+a0 makes the 'DOWN' world axis point up; I verified for a flat phone (a0=[0,0,+9.8]) the resulting DOWN column is [0,0,+1] (up). This yields a world frame mirrored along the vertical, so the initial body-to-world rotation (and hence the initial orientation quaternion seed) is reflected — gravity-projected accelerations and any double-integration in the world frame get the vertical/handedness wrong.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use DOWN = -a0/|a0| (or equivalently build from gravity = -specific_force). Re-derive EAST = cross(DOWN, mag) and NORTH = cross(EAST, DOWN) consistently and confirm det(R)=+1 with a known flat-phone case. Resolve the EAST=cross(m,a) vs cross(a,m) ordering against the chosen DOWN sign so the frame is a true right-handed NED.

bugs.title: Call site passes (acce, magnet) but get_body2world_rot signature is (m0, a0) — arguments swapped
bugs.description: initial_orientation = rotation_matrix_2_quaternion(get_body2world_rot(X[...acc_cols...], X[...mag_cols...])). The function is defined get_body2world_rot(m0, a0) (m0 = magnetometer first, a0 = accelerometer second), so the accelerometer is bound to m0 and the magnetometer to a0.
bugs.why_wrong: Inside the function EAST = cross(m0, a0) and DOWN = a0. With the arguments swapped, DOWN is built from the magnetometer (not gravity) and EAST = cross(acc, mag) instead of cross(mag, acc). The whole initial world frame is constructed from the wrong sensors, producing an essentially arbitrary seed rotation. Combined with the DOWN sign bug and the convention mismatch, the orientation seed is wrong three independent ways.
bugs.fix_sketch: Swap the call to get_body2world_rot(mag, acc) (or rename params and fix consistently). Add a keyword-argument call site (m0=mag, a0=acc) so the binding is explicit and cannot silently swap.

bugs.title: vec_norm returns a (1,1) array (not a scalar) for column-vector input, masking intent in module-level Theta
bugs.description: vec_norm(v) = np.sqrt(v.T@v). The module-level Theta path reshapes w to (3,1), so v.T@v is (1,1) and vec_norm returns a (1,1) array; this then broadcasts in `np.cos(u_b_norm/2)*np.eye(4) + np.sin(u_b_norm/2)/(u_b_norm/2)*W`.
bugs.why_wrong: The trig-of-an-array still broadcasts to the right shape here so it happens to work, but it is fragile: the function silently returns different shapes (scalar vs (1,1)) depending on whether the input is 1-D or a column, and any code expecting a Python float (e.g. a guard `if vec_norm(w) < eps`) would compare against a (1,1) array. The matrix_norm/vec_norm helpers should return scalars.
bugs.fix_sketch: Return float(np.linalg.norm(v.ravel())) (or np.sqrt((v*v).sum())). Standardize on np.linalg.norm to avoid the .T@v shape ambiguity.

bugs.title: Double-integration formula is physically wrong (spurious cumsum(acc**2) term)
bugs.description: p = np.cumsum(v, axis=1)*1/200 + np.cumsum(X[:,:,acc]**2, axis=1)*1/200**2/2. Position is computed as the cumulative sum of velocity plus a 'half integral of acceleration squared' term. The same line exists in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:130.
bugs.why_wrong: Correct discrete double integration of acceleration to position is p_t = sum_{k<=t} v_k * dt where v_k = sum_{j<=k} a_j * dt (i.e. p = cumsum(cumsum(a)*dt)*dt). The standard kinematic '+1/2 a t^2' refers to a*t^2 over a single interval, NOT acc**2. Squaring the acceleration (a**2) is dimensionally and physically meaningless (units of (m/s^2)^2), it is not part of any kinematic equation, it is always non-negative so it injects a monotonic drift into every axis, and it scales with dt^2/2 on top of an already-present cumsum(v)*dt. The comment 'plus half of the integral of acceleration squared' reveals the author conflated the (1/2)a t^2 term with integrating a^2. The acc**2 term must be removed entirely; p should be a pure double-integral of a.
bugs.fix_sketch: p = np.cumsum(v, axis=1) * (1/200)  # v already = cumsum(acc)*dt, so this is cumsum(cumsum(acc)*dt)*dt. Delete the + np.cumsum(acc**2)*dt^2/2 term.

bugs.title: Double integration runs on z-score-normalized acceleration (no physical units, gravity removed by whitening)
bugs.description: params_load_data has normalize=True. In utils.load_split_data the full feature matrix (including synced/acce) is passed through StandardScaler (mean 0, unit variance per column) BEFORE windowing and before preprocess_data. preprocess_data then rotates and double-integrates these normalized accelerations into v (line 133) and p (line 137). Same in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:126,130.
bugs.why_wrong: Integrating acceleration to get velocity/position is only meaningful in SI units (m/s^2). After per-axis StandardScaler the acc channel is dimensionless, zero-mean, unit-variance; the mean (which encodes gravity + the DC component that actually moves you) has been subtracted and each axis independently rescaled by an arbitrary factor. cumsum of a zero-mean whitened signal is a random-walk with no relation to true velocity/displacement, and the *1/200 dt factor is meaningless against unitless data. The 'informed' v and p features are therefore garbage. The integration (if intended as a physics prior) must be done on raw, gravity-compensated acceleration in m/s^2, before or independent of normalization.
bugs.fix_sketch: Compute v and p from raw (un-normalized), gravity-subtracted, world-frame acceleration; normalize the learned/raw input features separately from the physics-derived ones, or skip normalization on the acc channel used for integration.

bugs.title: scalar-first quaternion fed into scipy from_quat which expects scalar-last
bugs.description: orientations are built by rotation_matrix_2_quaternion (q[0]=scalar w, q[1:4]=x,y,z -> scalar-FIRST [w,x,y,z]) and propagated by Theta; they are then applied via R.from_quat(orientations[seq,i]).apply(...). scipy's Rotation.from_quat uses scalar-LAST ordering [x,y,z,w] by default. Same pattern in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:123.
bugs.why_wrong: Confirmed empirically: scipy 1.17 from_quat([1,0,0,0]) (a scalar-first identity) is interpreted as a 180-degree rotation about x, not identity. So every world-frame rotation is applying the wrong rotation (axes permuted/flipped), corrupting the world-frame acceleration that is then integrated. The quaternion must be reordered to [x,y,z,w] before from_quat (e.g. orientations[..., [1,2,3,0]]), or use scalar_first=True (newer scipy). NOTE: for the EKF/tango paths the dataset's stored quaternions also have their own convention (RoNIN tango_ori/ekf_ori are stored [w,x,y,z]); they too need reordering before from_quat.
bugs.fix_sketch: q_xyzw = orientations[seq,i][[1,2,3,0]]; R.from_quat(q_xyzw).apply(acc). Verify against dataset's documented quaternion order for tango_ori/ekf_ori.

bugs.title: Orientation key check uses wrong key name -> tango_ori never used, falls back to buggy gyro integrator
bugs.description: INPUT_FEATURES includes 'pose/tango_ori' (line 39), but the orientation selection tests `if 'synced/tango_ori' in col_locations['input']`. The key actually present is 'pose/tango_ori', so the test is always False and the code falls through to get_orientations(X), recomputing orientation by integrating the gyro instead of using the high-quality ground-truth tango orientation that was deliberately loaded.
bugs.why_wrong: The provided, accurate orientation (pose/tango_ori) is silently ignored; the script instead uses a home-grown, numerically broken gyro integrator (see Theta NaN/non-orthonormal bugs below) seeded from a magnetometer/accel triad. This both wastes the loaded feature and feeds a worse orientation into the world-frame rotation. Should be `if 'pose/tango_ori' in col_locations['input']` (mirroring the correct 'pose/ekf_ori' branch added in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:110).
bugs.fix_sketch: Change the key to 'pose/tango_ori' and select that slice, as done for ekf_ori in the EKF script.

bugs.title: Theta orientation-update matrix is non-orthonormal and NaNs on zero angular velocity
bugs.description: Theta returns cos(|u|/2)*I + (sin(|u|/2)/(|u|/2)) * W, where W=Omega(w) is built from the UN-normalized angular velocity w and |u| = |w|*dt. Confirmed empirically: with w=[0.1,0.2,0.3], Theta@Theta.T has diagonal 1.14 (not 1.0) so it is not norm-preserving; with w=[0,0,0] it returns all-NaN (0/0 from sin(0)/0).
bugs.why_wrong: The correct quaternion-update operator is cos(|u|/2)*I + sin(|u|/2) * (W/|W|) (i.e. the matrix term must use the unit rotation-axis matrix). Here the scale factor sin(|u|/2)/(|u|/2) is the sinc-style factor for w*dt, but W still carries the magnitude |w|*dt, so the rotor norm is wrong and the propagated quaternion is distorted (the per-step renormalization at line 112 fixes the quaternion's length but not the incorrect rotation it encodes). Zero/near-zero gyro samples (common when the phone is still) produce NaN that propagates through cumsum and the network. Note utils.Theta differs from the inline Theta defined in load_split_data (lines 312-334) which divides by w_norm instead of u_b_norm/2 — two inconsistent definitions of the same operator.
bugs.fix_sketch: Normalize W by its magnitude (or build Omega from w/|w|), and guard |w|->0 with a small-angle/identity fallback to avoid NaN. Reconcile the two Theta definitions.

bugs.title: Train/test target reference frames are inconsistent (mean-centering applied to train only)
bugs.description: In preprocess_data, when test==False the target is rebased per-window: y -= y[:, :1, :] (subtract the window's first position), then y = y[:,-1,:] is taken as the regression target (line 151). For test (test=True, line 160) the y-=y[:,:1,:] step is SKIPPED, so y[:,-1,:] is the absolute (un-rebased) final position. Later at plot time only the test labels get a single global shift y_test -= y_test[0] (line 302), and y_train gets none.
bugs.why_wrong: The model is trained to predict per-window relative displacement (final minus first position within the window), but at test time the target it is compared against is the absolute world position (minus only the very first test window's offset). These are different quantities with completely different magnitudes and statistics, so train and test/plot are measuring different targets. The reference frame must be identical across splits: apply the same per-window rebasing (y -= y[:, :1, :]) to test as to train (the EKF script repeats the identical bug at lines 55-56,144,153,295).
bugs.fix_sketch: Remove the `if test==False` guard so all splits rebase per-window identically; drop the ad-hoc y_test-=y_test[0] at plot time or apply it consistently.

bugs.title: Trajectory reconstruction cumsums shuffled, overlapping windows in arbitrary order
bugs.description: Windows are created with overlap=1 and seq_len=50 (stride = seq_len-overlap = 49, so windows are essentially non-overlapping-but-misaligned), then for the train/val split train_test_split(..., random_state=42) SHUFFLES the windows. The final trajectory is reconstructed by y_pred_test = np.cumsum(y_pred_test, axis=0) (and same for y_test, y_calced), i.e. summing per-window displacements in array order.
bugs.why_wrong: cumsum of per-window relative displacements only reconstructs a trajectory if (a) each value is a displacement over a contiguous segment and (b) the windows are in temporal order and tile the timeline without gaps/overlap. Here test windows have stride 49 within a 50-sample window (so consecutive windows share 1 sample and the displacement covers 49 of 50 steps — the cumsum drops/duplicates one step per window), and crucially the y_calced 'position' being summed is the per-window absolute final position (calced/position is cumsum within the window starting from ~0), not an inter-window delta — summing absolute end-positions across windows is meaningless. For train, train_test_split has shuffled the windows so cumsum runs over a random permutation, producing a nonsense path. The displacements must be true consecutive non-overlapping segment deltas, kept in temporal order (no shuffle) before cumsum.
bugs.fix_sketch: Do not shuffle the sequence dimension before trajectory reconstruction; ensure windows tile the timeline (stride == seq_len) and that the summed quantity is a per-window delta consistent with the window stride; reconstruct in original temporal order.

bugs.title: acc bias removal subtracts the first sample, forcing the first acceleration row to ~0 before integration
bugs.description: X[:, :, acc] -= X[:, :1, acc] subtracts each window's first accelerometer sample from all samples in that window (done in body frame, BEFORE the world-frame rotation and integration). Same in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:118.
bugs.why_wrong: This is an ad-hoc 'bias' removal that assumes the first sample is the true bias/gravity offset, which is false: the first sample contains real motion + gravity + noise. Subtracting it (a) zeroes out the genuine acceleration at t0, (b) removes the gravity vector inconsistently (gravity should be removed in the world frame after rotation, as a constant g on the down axis, not as the body-frame value of one arbitrary instant), and (c) since it is done before rotation, the subtracted constant is rotated together with the signal, so it does not even cancel a constant world-frame gravity. Combined with normalization (which already removed per-axis mean) this is double, physically incoherent de-biasing. Gravity should be removed in world frame (subtract [0,0,g]) using a proper orientation, on un-normalized data.
bugs.fix_sketch: Remove the first-sample subtraction; after rotating raw acc to world frame, subtract the gravity vector [0,0,9.81] (or use synced/linacce which is already gravity-compensated).

bugs.title: Normalization re-fits StandardScaler on test data (no train->test transfer; train/test scaled by different stats)
bugs.description: normalize_features always calls scaler.fit_transform(X) regardless of whether a scaler was passed. load_split_data calls it for test as normalize_features(X_test, scaler=scaler) intending to reuse train statistics, but because fit_transform is called unconditionally the passed scaler is overwritten and the test set is standardized on its own mean/variance.
bugs.why_wrong: Test (and the val split, which is carved out later) must be transformed with the TRAIN scaler's statistics. Re-fitting on test means train and test inputs live in different normalized spaces, so a model fit on train sees a distribution-shifted test set; it also leaks test statistics into the test features. Should be: if scaler is provided, call scaler.transform(X), not fit_transform.
bugs.fix_sketch: In normalize_features: `X_normalized = scaler.fit_transform(X) if fit_needed else scaler.transform(X)` — i.e. only fit when scaler was None.

bugs.title: Declared Transformer and RNN are dead code; forward() is a pure MLP (the 'transformer'/'informed' model isn't used)
bugs.description: Net.__init__ builds self.transformer = nn.Transformer(d_model=23, nhead=1, ...) and self.rnn = nn.RNN(...), but forward() only runs x = self.fc_in(x); x = self.fc_out(x) with both `self.transformer(x,x)` and `self.rnn(x)` commented out (lines 218-219). The flattened input (input_size*SEQ_LEN) is fed straight into Linear layers. Identical in Linear_informed_with_EKF.py:181-185,206-220.
bugs.why_wrong: The script is titled 'transformer_informed' and constructs a Transformer, but the actual computation is a multilayer perceptron over the flattened window; the temporal/sequence structure is destroyed by the reshape (line 150) and never modeled by attention. The Transformer/RNN params are allocated, counted, and saved but never receive gradients (they are disconnected from the loss). This is the literal 'compression' the user worries about: a 50x23 window is flattened and MLP'd into a 3-vector with no sequence model. Additionally nhead=1 on the never-used transformer means no multi-head attention even if it were wired in. Either wire the transformer into forward (and feed it [batch, seq, feat], not the flattened vector) or remove the unused modules and rename.
bugs.fix_sketch: If a sequence model is intended: keep X as [batch, SEQ_LEN, feat] (don't flatten at line 150), run self.transformer/rnn, take the last/pooled step; else delete the unused modules. Use nhead>1.

bugs.title: Single-sample inference without batch dim relies on accidental shape behavior; inconsistent train(batched)/infer(unbatched)
bugs.description: At eval, predictions are produced one sample at a time: model(torch.from_numpy(X_test[i]).float()) where X_test[i] is a 1-D vector of length input_size*SEQ_LEN (no batch dimension), looped over every row. Training used batched 2-D inputs. Same in EKF script 281-287.
bugs.why_wrong: Feeding a 1-D tensor to nn.Linear works only because Linear broadcasts over the last dim, so it happens not to crash for the pure-MLP path — but it is fragile, extremely slow (Python loop over up to ~67k/1.6M samples), and would break the moment the (declared) transformer/rnn path requiring a batch dim were enabled. It also bypasses any batchnorm/sequence semantics. Inference should pass batched tensors of shape [N, features] (or [N, seq, feat]) consistent with training.
bugs.fix_sketch: preds = model(torch.from_numpy(X_test).float()) in one (or chunked) batched call; keep the same input rank as training.

bugs.title: in-place mutation of shared col_locations across train/val/test calls; relative-index updates re-run each call
bugs.description: preprocess_data mutates the passed col_locations dict in place (col_locations['input']['calced/...'] = [X.shape[2]-10, ...]) and returns it; the same dict object is then passed into the val call (line 159) and the result is also used to index X_test reshaped at the end. The 'calced/*' offsets are recomputed from X.shape[2] each call.
bugs.why_wrong: Because col_locations is shared and mutated, the train call appends 'calced/orientations','calced/velocity','calced/position' to the SAME dict that is then handed to the val/test calls. On those later calls these keys already exist (harmless here since offsets are recomputed from the new X.shape[2]), but the pattern is brittle: any reader relying on col_locations to describe the ORIGINAL input width is now seeing post-concatenation indices, and the negative-offset scheme assumes exactly 10 appended columns (4 orient + 3 v + 3 p) — if INPUT_FEATURES changes the orientation width (e.g. 0 if no quat path), the -10/-6/-3 slicing silently misaligns. Should build a fresh col_locations copy per split and compute offsets from known widths.
bugs.fix_sketch: Deep-copy col_locations inside preprocess_data; derive appended-feature offsets from explicit widths (len(orient)+3+3) rather than hard-coded -10/-6/-3.

bugs.title: DataLoader shuffle=False makes batches temporally/structurally correlated (poor SGD, and interacts with the already-shuffled split)
bugs.description: dataloader_train uses shuffle=False. The training data was shuffled once by train_test_split(random_state=42), but within an epoch the order is then fixed across all 300 epochs.
bugs.why_wrong: With shuffle=False every epoch sees the identical batch composition and order, which biases AdamW's gradient estimates and can entrench batch-to-batch correlation; standard practice is shuffle=True for the training loader. Combined with the per-window shuffle from train_test_split, the temporal order needed for the cumsum trajectory reconstruction (bug above) is already destroyed for train. For training quality this should be shuffle=True; for trajectory reconstruction an unshuffled, temporally-ordered copy is needed separately.
bugs.fix_sketch: Set shuffle=True on the training DataLoader; keep a separate ordered array for trajectory plotting.

bugs.title: Learning rate 3e-6 (and 1e-6) is far too low for a fresh MLP of this size / 300 epochs
bugs.description: LEARNING_RATE = 0.000_003 (3e-6) with AdamW from scratch; Linear_informed_with_EKF.py uses 1e-6 with 1000 epochs.
bugs.why_wrong: For a randomly initialized multi-hidden-layer MLP (hidden_size 500-1000) with no weight init (the xavier_uniform_ init is commented out, lines 207-209), AdamW at 3e-6/1e-6 will barely move the weights over 300/1000 epochs, so the network likely underfits and the regression collapses toward the target mean — making the model effectively a constant predictor regardless of the input physics features. This is a tuning issue rather than a hard correctness bug, but at these values the 'learned' part of the pipeline contributes little. Typical AdamW LR here is ~1e-3 to 1e-4 with proper initialization.
bugs.fix_sketch: Enable weight initialization and raise LR to ~1e-3/1e-4; verify train loss actually decreases beyond the variance-of-target baseline.

bugs.title: calced/position used as 'calced' trajectory is per-window absolute, not comparable to cumsum'd predictions
bugs.description: y_calced_test takes the last-timestep calced/position of each window (the within-window double-integrated position, which starts at ~0 each window) and then cumsums it across windows (line 311) to overlay as the 'calced' baseline against the model and ground truth.
bugs.why_wrong: calced/position[:, -1] is the absolute displacement accumulated WITHIN one window (each window's integration restarts from zero because v and p are cumsum along axis=1 of that window). Summing these per-window end displacements across windows (cumsum axis=0) does not equal the true continuous trajectory — it adds independent per-window integrals as if they were inter-window deltas, with each window's velocity reset to 0 at its start (velocity continuity across windows is lost). So the 'calced' comparison curve is not a valid dead-reckoning trajectory and will not be on the same footing as either the (broken) ground truth or predictions. The physics baseline needs continuous velocity/position integration across the full sequence, not per-window resets summed.
bugs.fix_sketch: Integrate velocity/position continuously across the whole test sequence (carry v forward between windows) to build the dead-reckoning baseline, rather than cumsumming per-window absolute end positions.

bugs.title: Trajectory reconstruction (cumsum of per-window displacements) assumes stride == displacement span; drifts with overlap != 1
bugs.description: Each window's target is the displacement from window-start to window-end, spanning seq_len-1 raw samples (lines 358-373: y zeroed to window start, then [:, -1, :]). The reconstruction y_pred = y_pred + vstack([offset0, offset0 + cumsum(y_pred[:-1])]) then prepends offset0, i.e. it integrates each per-window displacement as if consecutive windows were laid end-to-end. That is only correct when the stride between window starts (seq_len - overlap) equals the displacement span (seq_len - 1), i.e. only when overlap == 1.
bugs.why_wrong: Correct behavior: the reconstructed absolute trajectory point for window i should be the true window-start position offset[i] plus the predicted within-window displacement, OR (if integrating step-by-step) the per-step displacement must cover exactly one stride. With overlap != 1 the windows overlap/skip, so cumulatively summing displacements that span seq_len-1 samples over-counts by (seq_len-1)/(seq_len-overlap) per step. Verified numerically: with seq_len=30, overlap=1 a perfect model reconstructs exactly; with seq_len=173, overlap=20 a perfect model's reconstructed x drifts 0,0,-19,-38,-57,... i.e. linear drift purely from the reconstruction formula. many_predictions.py uses overlap=20.
bugs.fix_sketch: Reconstruct predictions the same way as GT: y_pred_abs = predicted_displacement + offset[i] (use the known per-window start offsets, not cumsum). If a true dead-reckoning integration is wanted, make the per-window target the displacement over exactly one stride (seq_len-overlap samples) and cumsum those, with the offsets only used for the first point.

bugs.title: Prediction and ground-truth trajectories reconstructed by inconsistent formulas
bugs.description: y_pred (lines 532-534) is rebuilt by cumulatively summing the per-window displacements. q_gts (lines 536-538) is rebuilt by adding the per-window absolute offset pred_offset[i] to each per-window displacement (q_gts = disp + offset). These are two different reconstruction operators applied to prediction vs truth.
bugs.why_wrong: Correct behavior: pred and GT trajectories must be reconstructed with the identical operator so that ATE measures model error, not a difference in reconstruction math. Because GT uses the true per-window offsets but the prediction uses cumsum, even a perfect model only matches when overlap==1 (the coincidence noted in the previous bug). For overlap!=1, a perfect model gets nonzero ATE/RTE attributable entirely to the metric, not the model. Same inconsistent pair appears in one_prediction.py (621-632) and many_predictions.py (583-591, 960-968).
bugs.fix_sketch: Apply one reconstruction to both: either GT also via cumsum of its own per-window displacements, or (preferred) prediction also via displacement+offset. Then ATE = error of the model only.

bugs.title: ATE computed as mean of per-point Euclidean distances, not RoNIN RMSE
bugs.description: ATE = np.sqrt(((q_gts - y_pred)**2).sum(axis=1)).mean() takes the per-point L2 distance and then the arithmetic MEAN over points.
bugs.why_wrong: RoNIN's ATE is the root-mean-square of the per-point position error: sqrt(mean(||p_pred - p_gt||^2)), not mean(||...||). These differ (e.g. distances {5,0,10}: code gives 5.0, RMSE gives 6.45). The reported ATE is systematically lower than the RoNIN ATE and is not comparable to published RoNIN numbers. Same in one_prediction.py (638) and many_predictions.py (598, 845, 975).
bugs.fix_sketch: ATE = np.sqrt((((q_gts - y_pred)**2).sum(axis=1)).mean()) (move .mean() inside the sqrt).

bugs.title: RTE formula in pred_pos_lstm.py is a meaningless fraction-scaling of ATE
bugs.description: RTE = ATE * (60*(1/dt)/seq_len) / (Ntest/seq_len) if Ntest/seq_len <= 60 else ATE. The factor evaluates to (#windows-per-60s)/(#total-windows) = fraction of the trajectory contained in one minute. So RTE = ATE * (1-minute-fraction-of-trajectory), and for any realistic run (Ntest/seq_len = 2166 > 60) the branch collapses to RTE = ATE.
bugs.why_wrong: RoNIN RTE is the position drift accumulated over a fixed 1-minute sub-trajectory (averaged over all 1-min segments), independent of total trajectory length. Multiplying ATE by the fraction of the trajectory that fits in a minute has no physical meaning and shrinks ATE arbitrarily with trajectory length; the else-branch just aliases RTE to ATE. The metric does not measure relative/segment drift at all.
bugs.fix_sketch: Replace with the standard RoNIN RTE: for each contiguous 1-minute (60s/dt samples => 60/dt/stride windows) segment, compute the endpoint position error (or RMSE over that segment) and average across segments.

bugs.title: RTE loop drops the last minute block but divides by Nmins (off-by-one), and is windowed mean-ATE not RoNIN drift
bugs.description: for min in range(Nmins - 1): RTE += ATE_vec[minute_idx*min : minute_idx*(min+1)].mean(); then RTE /= Nmins. It sums Nmins-1 block means but normalizes by Nmins. Also ATE_vec is the per-point absolute error along the reconstructed trajectory, so each block contributes its mean absolute error, not the segment drift.
bugs.why_wrong: Two problems: (1) Off-by-one normalization: sums Nmins-1 terms, divides by Nmins, biasing RTE low by a factor ~(Nmins-1)/Nmins and silently ignoring the final minute of data. (2) Semantics: RoNIN RTE measures drift over a 1-min window (typically the endpoint error of a sub-trajectory of fixed length), whereas this averages the already-accumulated absolute trajectory error within each minute block — which conflates global ATE drift with relative drift. Same pattern at lines 725-731 (plot_testing), and many_predictions.py 977-983 / pred_pos_lstm_many_predictions has the same in do_testing.
bugs.fix_sketch: Iterate range(Nmins) (or normalize by the number of blocks actually summed), and compute per-segment relative error (reset each segment to its own start, measure endpoint/RMS error within the segment) rather than the mean of the cumulative absolute error.

bugs.title: Unguarded RTE /= Nmins divides by zero for sub-60s test trajectories
bugs.description: In do_many_tests, RTE /= Nmins has no 'if Nmins > 0' guard (unlike the do_simple_testing path at 645-648). Nmins = floor(Ntest*dt/60).
bugs.why_wrong: If a test clip is shorter than 60s (Ntest*dt < 60 => Nmins == 0), this raises ZeroDivisionError / yields inf-nan, and the preceding loop range(Nmins-1)=range(-1) is empty so RTE stays 0 before the divide. Verified: Ntest=10000 at dt=1/200 gives Nseconds=50, Nmins=0. The do_testing path in many_predictions.py (line 983) has the same unguarded divide.
bugs.fix_sketch: Add the same Nmins>0 guard used at lines 645-648, falling back to RTE = ATE*60/Nseconds for short clips.

bugs.title: Orientation filters seeded with a 3D ground-truth POSITION as the initial quaternion q0
bugs.description: q_0 = y_train[0, 0, :] is passed as q0 to Madgwick/Mahony/EKF. But output_features = ['pose/tango_pos'] (line 204), so y_train[0,0,:] is the initial 3D position vector, not a unit quaternion.
bugs.why_wrong: AHRS filters require q0 to be a 4-element unit quaternion (initial orientation), e.g. from pose/tango_ori or acc2q(acc[0]). Feeding a 3-element position is dimensionally wrong (length 3 vs 4) and not normalized; the filter either errors or silently initializes orientation to garbage, corrupting every downstream filtered-orientation feature. Identical bug in one_prediction.py (253) and many_predictions.py (161).
bugs.fix_sketch: Set q_0 from an actual orientation source (acc2q of the first accelerometer sample, or the first pose/tango_ori quaternion), and ensure it is a length-4 unit quaternion.

bugs.title: Madgwick/Mahony/EKF run over concatenated train+test as a single chain -> train->test state leakage
bugs.description: X = np.vstack((X_train, X_test)) (line 260), then the IMU streams are extracted and a single Madgwick/Mahony/EKF filter is instantiated over the whole concatenated array; results are split back via X[:Ntrain_sequences] / X[Ntrain_sequences:] (296-297). The AHRS filters integrate sequentially from q0 forward, so the orientation state at the end of the training segment carries into the first test samples.
bugs.why_wrong: Test features must be computed without any information flowing from training data. Because the filter is one continuous recursive estimator over [train; test], the test orientation features depend on the training trajectory's integrated state — a leakage of train into the test feature stream. The disabled 'if 0:' block at 299-332 shows the author had a per-split version (separate filters per X_train/X_test) but it is dead. Same in one_prediction.py (252-289 active, 291-324 dead) and many_predictions.py (160-197).
bugs.fix_sketch: Run the filters separately on X_train and X_test (and ideally per-recording), each with its own correct q0; never vstack train and test before filtering. Re-enable a corrected version of the per-split loop.

bugs.title: Filters integrate a reshaped windowed stream that duplicates/reorders boundary samples
bugs.description: X_gyro = X[:, :, gyro_idx].reshape(-1, 3) (and acc/mag) flattens the windowed array (Nseq, seq_len, 3) back to a per-sample stream by concatenating windows. But windows were built with overlap=1 (stride seq_len-1), so consecutive windows share their boundary sample; the reshaped stream therefore duplicates the shared sample and breaks true time-continuity across window boundaries.
bugs.why_wrong: An AHRS filter assumes a continuous, monotically-sampled IMU stream at fixed dt. Verified: with seq_len=4, overlap=1, the reshaped stream is 0,1,2,3,3,4,5,6,6,7,... (boundary samples 3,6,9 duplicated) instead of 0,1,2,...,19. Each duplicated sample injects a spurious zero-dt update and the per-window resets create discontinuities, so the integrated orientations are wrong. The subsequent .reshape(-1, seq_len, 4) re-windows these corrupted quaternions. The dt is also still 1/200 despite duplicate samples.
bugs.fix_sketch: Run the filters on the original un-windowed, de-duplicated continuous IMU arrays (the pre-create_sequences stream), then window the resulting quaternions; or reconstruct the contiguous stream before filtering.

bugs.title: use_truth_input leaks ground-truth position into the model input
bugs.description: When use_truth_input is True, output_features[0] (pose/tango_pos, the GT position) is appended as an input feature (222-223). Then X[:, 1:, -Noutput:] are zeroed (343-344), leaving X[:, 0, -Noutput:] = the absolute GT position at each window start as a model input. At test time (486-498) only after i>10 is the previous prediction substituted for the first timestep; for i<=10 the true GT position is fed.
bugs.why_wrong: Feeding the ground-truth position (even only the window-start value) as an input is target leakage: the network receives a GT-derived signal that is unavailable at inference and is highly correlated with the quantity being predicted. At test time the first 11 windows are fed true GT positions outright. This inflates apparent accuracy. (use_truth_input defaults to False here, but the path is wired as a usable mode.) Same in one_prediction.py (208-209, 333-335, 580-592).
bugs.fix_sketch: Never include the target/GT position as an input. If an autoregressive previous-position input is intended, feed only the model's own previous prediction (or a measured surrogate) from step 0, never the ground truth.

bugs.title: 'start' offset chosen for the test file is reused for all training slices
bugs.description: In load_much_data, 'start' is assigned only inside the 'if dir in test_dir' branch (line 180, possibly a random offset). Because dirs is sorted and test_dir=dirs[:1] is iterated first, 'start' is defined by the test file, then reused as the slice start for the training directories (lines 198, 203). The vstack branches for additional dirs use [:N] (start 0) instead, so even within a split the slicing is inconsistent.
bugs.why_wrong: Each training directory should be sliced from its own (start=0 or its own random offset), not from the offset randomly drawn for the test recording. As written, the first train dir is sliced [start:start+N] using the test file's random_start, while subsequent train dirs use [:N]. This is fragile coupling and, with random_start=True, makes the training slice depend on the test file. If test_dir were ever not first in iteration order, 'start' would be undefined (NameError).
bugs.fix_sketch: Initialize start=0 before the loop and compute a per-directory start inside each branch; do not let the test branch's start leak into the train branch.

bugs.title: Undefined variable trial_no in savetxt
bugs.description: np.savetxt(f'predictions_arr{trial_no}.txt', ...) references trial_no, which is never defined; the defined variable is n_trial (line 121).
bugs.why_wrong: This raises NameError the first time do_simple_testing reaches line 627, aborting the test/metric section. The intended variable is n_trial.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use n_trial (or define trial_no).

bugs.title: Validation set is a contiguous tail of the same subjects/recordings as train (in-distribution model selection)
bugs.description: train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=Nval_fraction, shuffle=False) takes the last 20% of training windows as validation. Those windows come from the same training directories/subjects (load_much_data stacks all train dirs).
bugs.why_wrong: Validation used for early stopping / model selection is not a held-out subject, so val loss overstates generalization to new subjects (only dirs[0] test set is a true holdout). With overlap=1 the val tail windows are also temporally adjacent to (and share a boundary sample with) the last train window. Acceptable as an intentional in-distribution val, but worth flagging as a generalization-measurement weakness.
bugs.fix_sketch: Hold out validation by subject/recording, or at least leave a gap of >=seq_len samples between the train tail and val head to avoid window overlap.

bugs.title: Training-loss print divided by seq_len (cosmetic but misleading), absent in other files
bugs.description: Loss is printed as running_loss/n_minibatches/seq_len. With pred_only_last=True the criterion already operates on a single (B,2) target per window, so MSE is per-window, not per-sequence; dividing by seq_len (=30) is an arbitrary rescale.
bugs.why_wrong: The MSELoss here is over the last-step target only, so there is no seq_len factor to remove; dividing by seq_len makes the printed loss 30x smaller than the actual optimization objective and not comparable to one_prediction.py / many_predictions.py which print running_loss/n_minibatches. Purely a reporting bug (does not affect gradients) but misleads loss-curve comparison and the 'worsens with more epochs' debugging noted in the TODO.
bugs.fix_sketch: Print running_loss/n_minibatches (drop /seq_len) to match the actual objective and the other scripts.

bugs.title: many_predictions Net.forward feeds full sequence to the head but reconstruction still cumsums last-step displacements
bugs.description: Net.forward has x[:, -1, :] commented out (line 82), so it returns a per-timestep output (B, seq_len, out). Training targets are full per-window sequences (load_and_prepare_data keeps y as (B, seq_len, 2), lines 200-213). But at test (do_testing) only the last step is kept (pred.append(outputs[:,-1,:]), line 569) and pred_true = y_test[:,-1,:] (548), then the cumsum reconstruction (585-587) is applied.
bugs.why_wrong: The model is trained to predict the relative position at every timestep within a window (a sequence-to-sequence within-window task), but evaluation reduces to the last step and feeds it into the same overlap-sensitive cumsum reconstruction (overlap=20, seq_len=173 => the linear-drift bug above applies in full force). The train/test reduction mismatch plus the overlap=20 cumsum makes reported many_predictions trajectories unreliable even if training converges.
bugs.fix_sketch: Decide on one reduction: if predicting per-step relative positions, reconstruct by adding each window's last-step displacement to that window's true start offset (no cumsum), and keep overlap consistent between displacement span and stride.

bugs.title: FourVectorLoss arccos(|cos_sim|) has a singular (NaN) gradient at the optimum
bugs.description: loss = arccos(|cos_similarity|).sum()/batch_size. The derivative d/du arccos(u) = -1/sqrt(1-u^2) diverges as u->1, i.e. exactly when the predicted quaternion aligns with the target (cos_sim -> 1). Backprop then produces inf/NaN gradients. Verified: q1=q2=[1,0,0,0] gives loss 0.0 but grad [nan,nan,nan,nan].
bugs.why_wrong: The correct geodesic angular distance between unit quaternions is well-defined, but its arccos form is non-differentiable at coincidence. A NaN-safe loss clamps the argument away from +/-1 (e.g. acos(clamp(cos,-1+eps,1-eps))) or, better, uses 1-cos^2 / 1-|cos| / the squared-chordal distance which are smooth at the optimum. Taking torch.abs() to fold the double-cover also kinks the gradient at cos_sim=0.
bugs.fix_sketch: Replace with phi4-style 1-|<q1,q2>| (per-sample) or acos(clamp(|cos|, max=1-1e-6)); clamp before arccos and avoid the .sum()/batch_size (use mean). Also the explicit .cpu() of q1/q2 (lines 114-115) forces the loss off the model device every step.

bugs.title: phi2 loss collapses the whole batch to one scalar and picks a single global q/-q sign
bugs.lines: 294-295 (CustomLoss.phi2, cell 7); identical copy in quaternions_loss_func.ipynb cell 4 lines 184-185
bugs.description: phi2 returns aggregate(torch.min(torch.norm(q1-q2), torch.norm(q1+q2))). torch.norm with no dim/keepdim computes a single Frobenius norm over the ENTIRE (N,4) batch, returning a scalar. So min(||Q1-Q2||_all, ||Q1+Q2||_all) chooses ONE antipodal sign for the whole batch at once, and aggregate() (mean of a scalar) is a no-op. Verified shapes are torch.Size([]).
bugs.why_wrong: A per-sample quaternion loss must compute the distance for each sample and resolve the q vs -q double-cover per sample (min over sign should be inside a per-row norm: torch.minimum(norm(q1-q2,dim=1), norm(q1+q2,dim=1))). As written, the loss is dominated by the global scale of the batch and cannot represent that some samples need the + sign and others the - sign. This phi2 is the loss used for ALL the headline LSTM/GRU/RNN orientation results, so the reported 'validation loss 190/250/310' numbers are this malformed scalar.
bugs.fix_sketch: Compute per-row norms: d = torch.minimum(torch.norm(q1-q2,dim=1), torch.norm(q1+q2,dim=1)); then aggregate over dim 0. Same fix conceptually needed wherever phi2 is reused.

bugs.title: phi5 Frobenius norm reduces over the whole batch instead of per-sample
bugs.description: phi5 = aggregate(torch.norm(I[None] - bmm(R1,R2^T), p='fro')). torch.norm(..., p='fro') with no dim reduces the batched (N,3,3) tensor to a single scalar (verified shape torch.Size([])), so the rotation-matrix chordal distance is summed across all samples into one number before aggregate(), again making aggregate() a no-op and destroying per-sample structure.
bugs.why_wrong: Frobenius distance between rotation matrices should be computed per sample (dim=(-2,-1)) then aggregated. As written phi5 is one global magnitude, not a mean over samples.
bugs.fix_sketch: torch.norm(I[None]-bmm(R1,R2.transpose(-2,-1)), p='fro', dim=(-2,-1)) -> shape (N,), then aggregate.

bugs.title: Recurrent nets are fed sequences of length 1 (no temporal context)
bugs.description: train_data = torch.cat((gyro,acc,mag,Q_1,Q_2,Q_ekf,q_pred), dim=1) has shape (num_samples, F). Then input_size = train_data.shape[1] = F, and train_data = train_data.view(num_samples, -1, input_size). With the second dim being input_size=F, the inferred seq dimension (-1) is 1. Verified: view(num_samples,-1,F) yields seq_len=1.
bugs.why_wrong: An LSTM/GRU/RNN with bidirectional=True is built to consume a temporal window, but here every 'sequence' is a single timestep, so the recurrence and bidirectionality are inert and the model is effectively a per-sample MLP over concatenated features. This is the core 'compression' of a high-rate window into one estimate, and it is not performing any sequence reduction at all. It also means none of these models use the 200Hz temporal structure the project is about.
bugs.fix_sketch: Build true windows: reshape to (num_windows, seq_len, n_features_per_step) so input_size = features-per-timestep and dim 1 = seq_len. The cat over dim=1 of per-feature columns conflates feature axis with time.

bugs.title: Predicted quaternions are never normalized to unit norm at the network output
bugs.description: Every orientation network returns a raw 4-vector from a final Linear layer with no normalization. The CustomLoss has a 'normal' flag but all headline configs run normal=False (LSTM/GRU/RNN cells set normal=False; quat_to_rot only normalizes inside phi5). pred_ori_lstm/pred_ori_2_lstm use plain L1Loss against unit-norm ground truth with no unit-norm projection or penalty.
bugs.why_wrong: An orientation quaternion must lie on the unit 3-sphere. Regressing an unconstrained 4-vector under L1/L2/phi2 lets the network shrink magnitude to reduce loss without representing a valid rotation, and the resulting quaternion cannot be converted to a rotation without ambiguity. The model should either normalize the output (q/||q||) before the loss / before use, or add a unit-norm penalty.
bugs.fix_sketch: Append q = q / q.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) in forward (or normalize both args in the loss for every config), and/or add a (||q||-1)^2 regularizer.

bugs.title: Analytical Theta quaternion-update matrix is not orthonormal; norm drifts and is not renormalized
bugs.lines: 452-461 (module-level Theta used by the notebooks); near-duplicate inside load_split_data 312-334
bugs.description: Theta = cos(|u|/2)*I + sin(|u|/2)/(|u|/2) * Omega(w) with u=w*dt and Omega built from the RAW w. The exact norm-preserving update is cos(theta/2)*I + sin(theta/2)/|w| * Omega(w) with theta=|w|dt. The code's off-diagonal scale sin(|u|/2)/(|u|/2) = sin(|w|dt/2)/(|w|dt/2) differs from the correct 1/|w| by a factor 2/dt (=400 at dt=1/200). The notebooks paper over this with factor=.0025 (~dt/2) applied to w, explicitly commented 'has been set arbitrarily'. Verified the resulting matrix M satisfies M^T M ~ 1.000087*I (not I), so iterating drifts the quaternion norm 1.0 -> 1.24 over 5000 steps.
bugs.why_wrong: A quaternion kinematic integrator must apply an orthonormal (norm-preserving) update. The factor=.0025 only approximately cancels the scale error and is w-magnitude dependent, so the integration is biased and accumulates norm error; the per-step renormalization that would mask it (y_pred_NN[...] /= np.linalg.norm) is commented out in quaternion_update_anton_new.ipynb (cell 11, line 975).
bugs.fix_sketch: Use the exact form theta=|w|*dt; q_{k+1} = (cos(theta/2) I + sin(theta/2)/|w| * Omega(w)) q_k (guarding |w|~0), drop the arbitrary factor, and renormalize each step.

bugs.title: StandardScaler is re-fit on the test set instead of reusing the train scaler
bugs.description: normalize_features always calls scaler.fit_transform(X) even when a fitted scaler is passed in (the scaler argument is only used to decide whether to construct a new one, never to transform). So load_split_data normalizes X_test with X_test's own mean/std rather than the training statistics. Verified: passing the train scaler still yields test mean ~0 (re-fit).
bugs.why_wrong: Test/inference data must be transformed with the parameters learned on training data. Re-fitting on test gives the model test-distribution information at evaluation and makes train/test features inconsistently scaled, invalidating the reported orientation losses across all six files (all use normalize=True paths via load_split_data, except the quaternion_update notebooks which set normalize=False).
bugs.fix_sketch: if scaler is None: scaler=StandardScaler(); X=scaler.fit_transform(X) else: X=scaler.transform(X).

bugs.title: Autoregressive test feedback broadcasts batch-element-0's prediction to all samples
bugs.description: On test, inputs[:,0,ori_cols] = y_pred_tensor.reshape(B,seq_len,No)[0, -1]. The RHS indexes batch element 0, last timestep -> shape (No,), which then broadcasts the SAME sample-0 quaternion into the orientation slot of EVERY row in the batch. Verified broadcast fills all rows identically.
bugs.why_wrong: Closed-loop autoregression should feed each sample its own previous prediction (RHS should be [:, -1] -> (B,No)), and should also feed the temporally-adjacent prediction, not a cross-sample one. As written, every test sample is conditioned on the previous batch's first sample, corrupting the trajectory-style evaluation.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use y_pred_tensor.reshape(B,seq_len,No)[:, -1] and ensure batch ordering corresponds to time (test_loader shuffle=False is correct, but batch_size=1 vs the >0 branch shapes need to be reconciled).

bugs.title: Test-time loop mutates the held-out X_test tensor in place during autoregression
bugs.description: for i in range(X_test.shape[0]): if i>0: X_test[i,-4:] = torch.tensor(y_pred[i-1]); y_pred.append(net(X_test[i])...). This overwrites the ground-truth previous-orientation feature stored in X_test with the model's own previous prediction, permanently corrupting the test tensor (no copy). quaternion_update_anton_new.ipynb cell 10 lines 897-900 has the same in-place mutation.
bugs.why_wrong: Beyond the autoregression intent, mutating X_test in place means any re-run uses corrupted data, and the held-out set no longer contains its original inputs. The feedback should be written into a local copy. Note the cleaner cell 11 version (lines 962-975) builds a fresh X_line per step and does NOT mutate X_test, confirming this is an accidental mutation in the earlier cells.
bugs.fix_sketch: Operate on X_test.clone() or build inputs per step as in cell 11; never assign into the dataset tensor.

bugs.title: Sequence windows stride by seq_len-overlap, not by 1 (sparse, near-disjoint windows)
bugs.description: create_sequences steps range(0, N-seq+1, seq_length-overlap). With the orientation scripts' overlap=1, seq_len=5 the stride is 4 (windows start 0,4,8,12...); the load_split_data default overlap=0 gives stride seq_len (fully disjoint). 'overlap' is a misnomer: overlap=1 means windows overlap by 1 sample, not slide by 1.
bugs.why_wrong: For a 200Hz window->one-orientation reduction, neighbouring windows normally slide by 1 (stride 1, overlap seq_len-1) to use all data and give smooth trajectories. Here most timesteps appear in only one window and the effective sample count is reduced ~seq_len-fold; combined with the y-target handling this also changes which target each window predicts. It is at least an unintentional, under-documented choice.
bugs.fix_sketch: Make stride explicit (step = max(1, seq_len - overlap)) and document that overlap is the number of shared samples; for dense training use stride 1 (overlap=seq_len-1).

bugs.title: load_much_data reuses the test 'start' offset for the first train directory and mixes random/zero starts
bugs.description: The test branch sets start (0 or random 0..20000) and slices test data [start:start+N_test]. The train branch (elif) then reads new_data_dict[key][start:start+N_points_per_dir] using the SAME 'start' for the first train dir, but the vstack branch for later dirs uses [:N_points_per_dir] (start=0). Because dirs are sorted and test_dir=dirs[:1] is processed first, 'start' leaks across branches; if random_start picks a large value the first train dir can be offset differently from the rest.
bugs.why_wrong: Train and test windows should be sliced with independent, intentional offsets; the shared mutable 'start' couples them and makes the first train directory inconsistent with the others. There is also no guard that start+N_points_per_dir fits the first train file (only the test slice is bounds-checked at 181-182).
bugs.fix_sketch: Use separate start_test and start_train variables, bounds-check both, and apply the chosen start consistently to all train dirs (or none).

bugs.title: Display sign-flip uses ground truth (incl. test region) to pick a single global double-cover sign
bugs.lines: cell 1, lines 44-45 (plot_quaternions); identical in quaternions_LSTM_GRU_RNN.ipynb cell 2 lines 45-46
bugs.description: if np.linalg.norm(predictions-tango_ori) > np.linalg.norm(predictions+tango_ori): predictions = -predictions. This compares predictions to ground truth over the whole series (train+test) and flips the entire prediction array's sign once. It is cosmetic (inside a plotting function, executed per-axis inside the loop so it can flip differently across subplots), but it uses GT to choose the antipode and applies one global sign rather than per-sample.
bugs.why_wrong: Resolving q vs -q for visualization is reasonable, but doing it globally with test GT, and recomputing inside the i-loop (so predictions may be flipped on some axes and not others within the same figure), makes plots misleading. It does not affect training metrics.
bugs.fix_sketch: Resolve sign per sample once before plotting (sign = where(sum(pred*gt,axis=1)<0, -1, 1)); do it outside the per-axis loop.

bugs.title: Module-level utils.Theta quaternion-update matrix is not norm/orthogonality-preserving (wrong Omega scale + wrong denominator)
bugs.description: The module-level Omega(w) (lines 423-436) builds the 4x4 skew matrix WITHOUT the 1/2 factor that the standard quaternion kinematic operator requires, and Theta (lines 452-461) uses sin(u_b_norm/2)/(u_b_norm/2)*W. Numerically I verified Theta@Theta.T = 1.98*I (not I) and det=3.92, and applying Theta to a unit quaternion gives norm 1.407 instead of 1. So each integration step inflates the quaternion norm by ~40% and rotates by roughly double the intended angle. matrix_norm(W) (line 459) is computed and then discarded (dead). The correct closed-form exponential map is q_{k+1} = [cos(|w|dt/2) I + sin(|w|dt/2)/|w| * Omega_half(w)] q_k where Omega_half already contains the 1/2, i.e. the sin term must be divided by |w| (not |w|dt/2) and Omega must carry the 0.5. The notebook's OWN inner copy of Theta inside load_split_data (utils.py lines 285-334) gets this right (0.5 factor in Omega, divides by w_norm) and I verified IT is orthonormal. So the two Thetas disagree and the wrong one is the one imported by the baselines.
bugs.why_wrong: A proper quaternion-update operator must be orthogonal (preserve unit norm) so that integrating gyro keeps a valid unit quaternion. This one scales norm by ~1.4 per step, so over a 100-step window the orientation quaternion explodes (or has to be renormalized away, destroying the rotation magnitude). The angle is also ~2x too large because of the missing 0.5.
bugs.fix_sketch: Delete the duplicate module-level Omega/Theta and use a single correct version: Omega with the 0.5 factor (as in the inner copy) and Theta = cos(|w|dt/2) I + (sin(|w|dt/2)/|w|) * Omega(w). Or build the update quaternion directly from the rotvec w*dt via the exponential map. Import the one canonical Theta everywhere (kalman_filter_anton, transformer_informed).

bugs.title: Body->world rotation assigns DOWN = +accelerometer, but resting accelerometer points UP (frame vertically inverted)
bugs.description: get_body2world_rot sets DOWN = a0 (line 479, with the author's own comment 'maybe a minus sign is needed'). A stationary IMU measures specific force = -gravity, i.e. it reads ~+9.81 along the UP direction, not down. So DOWN is set to the up vector and the resulting frame is reflected/inverted about the vertical. Also NORTH = cross(EAST, DOWN) with EAST = cross(m, a) compounds the sign error. bodyFrame_to_worldFrame.ipynb cell 2-3 explicitly compares the resulting quaternion to tango_ori[0] to sanity-check it, which is exactly where this inversion would show up. The same buggy function is copy-pasted into transformer_informed.py and used in both transformer notebooks' forward() to compute the initial orientation.
bugs.why_wrong: RoNIN/Tango world frame is gravity-aligned (z up or NED). Defining DOWN as the +specific-force direction flips the vertical axis, so every acceleration subsequently rotated 'to world' has its vertical (and, through the cross products, horizontal) components mis-signed. Initial orientation handed to the integrator/network is wrong from sample zero.
bugs.fix_sketch: Use DOWN = -a0/|a0| (gravity direction) at rest, recompute EAST = cross(DOWN, m) or cross(m, DOWN) consistently, NORTH = cross(EAST, DOWN), and verify R against tango_ori on a static segment before trusting it. Make the row/column convention (R vs R.T) explicit and tested.

bugs.title: Double-integration baseline never removes gravity (uses synced/acce, not linacce)
bugs.description: Cell 4 does a_directed = quat_2_rotation_matrix(q_pred[i]) @ a[i] then v += a_directed*dt and p += v*dt + 0.5*a_directed*dt**2, where a = data['synced/acce'] (raw specific force including gravity, ~9.81 magnitude at rest). No gravity vector is subtracted before integration. I verified that a constant 9.81 m/s^2 double-integrates to 1.23 m of position drift in just 0.5 s (100 steps at 200 Hz), growing quadratically. The dataset provides synced/linacce (linear/gravity-removed acceleration) and synced/grav exactly for this; neither is used here.
bugs.why_wrong: Position from acceleration requires the gravity (specific-force-at-rest) component removed in the world frame, i.e. a_world - g_world, before double integration. Otherwise the estimate is dominated by a deterministic g*t^2/2 parabola, not motion. The orientation must also be accurate enough to cancel g in world frame, which it is not (see the factor=.002 and Theta bugs).
bugs.fix_sketch: Either integrate synced/linacce, or subtract the world-frame gravity vector ([0,0,+/-9.81]) from the rotated acceleration each step: a_world = R@a_raw - g_world. Verify the resting trajectory stays put before integrating real motion.

bugs.title: Quaternion integration scales gyro by an arbitrary 'factor' (~.002) that freezes orientation
bugs.description: The integration multiplies the gyro reading by factor=.002 (commented 'has been set arbitrarily') before forming the update: Theta(w[i]*factor, dt). This shrinks the per-step rotation angle to ~0.2% of the true angular increment, so the predicted orientation is essentially frozen at q0. The same arbitrary factor appears commented in utils.py lines 470-472. It appears to be a hack to mask the wrong Theta scaling (bug above) blowing up the quaternion. position_estimate / transformer paths use Theta(w, dt=1/200) without the factor and would instead suffer the norm blow-up.
bugs.why_wrong: The angular increment is w*dt with dt=1/200; there is no physical justification for an extra 0.002 multiplier. With it, the integrated orientation never tracks rotation; without it (and with the buggy Theta) the quaternion explodes. The real fix is the correct Theta, then factor must be removed.
bugs.fix_sketch: Remove factor entirely and use the corrected, orthonormal Theta with the proper dt. Validate predicted quaternion against tango_ori over the window.

bugs.title: EKF measurement is set equal to the prediction, so innovation is identically zero and the filter never corrects
bugs.lines: cell 8 (def ekf: z = x_pred; y = z - observation_model(x_pred))
bugs.description: Inside ekf(), the 'measurement' is z = x_pred and the innovation is y = z - observation_model(x_pred) = x_pred - x_pred = 0 (observation_model is identity). The Kalman gain K is computed but multiplies a zero innovation, so x_update = x_pred always; the update step is a no-op and the EKF degenerates to open-loop dead reckoning. Additional problems in the same cell: accel is scaled by an arbitrary /100 (accel_measurements = a[:N]/100), gyro is not scaled; state_transition uses scipy Rotation.from_quat/as_quat which expect (x,y,z,w) ordering while the state is initialized x[-4:]=q_tango[0] and the rest of the codebase uses (w,x,y,z) (rotation_matrix_2_quaternion/quat_2_rotation_matrix), a convention mismatch; and pos is updated with raw body-frame accel (gravity not removed, not rotated to world) so even the propagation is wrong.
bugs.why_wrong: An EKF must fuse an external measurement that differs from the prediction; the innovation drives the correction. Feeding the prediction back as the measurement makes the update vacuous. There is no actual position/orientation observation (e.g. tango pose, ZUPT, magnetometer heading) wired in.
bugs.fix_sketch: Supply a real measurement vector z (e.g. tango_pos/tango_ori or a pseudo-measurement like zero-velocity updates), with an H that maps state to that measurement. Fix the accel scaling (use m/s^2, remove gravity, rotate to world). Pick one quaternion convention and convert at the scipy boundary.

bugs.title: Transformer test-time trajectory reconstruction iterates over the batch dimension, so cumulative accumulation is a no-op
bugs.lines: cell 6 (accumulated_preds loop); identical in transformer_2_anton.ipynb cell 0
bugs.description: predictions = net(N_test) has shape (batch=1, seq, 3). The reconstruction 'for pred in predictions: accumulated_preds.append(pred + accumulated_preds[-1][-1] if accumulated_preds else pred)' iterates over the FIRST axis, which is the batch dimension of size 1. I verified the loop runs exactly once, so accumulated_preds == predictions and the subsequent reshape(-1,3) just flattens the single window. The intended behavior — turning per-step position deltas into an absolute trajectory by cumulative summation along the time axis — never happens. So the headline 'compression -> trajectory' step does nothing.
bugs.why_wrong: If the network outputs per-timestep deltas, the trajectory is np.cumsum over the time (sequence) axis, not over batch. As written, the model output is interpreted directly as absolute position, contradicting the y-preprocessing that subtracts the first value (treating y as relative).
bugs.fix_sketch: Decide whether the target is absolute position or per-step delta. If delta, do np.cumsum(predictions[0], axis=0) over the sequence axis (and integrate velocity properly). If absolute, drop the accumulation entirely. Make train target and test reconstruction consistent.

bugs.title: Pure-transformer PositionPredictor has no positional encoding -> permutation-invariant over time
bugs.lines: cell 3 (PositionPredictor; transformer_encoder then fc1/fc2, forward(src) passes src directly)
bugs.description: PositionPredictor feeds src straight into nn.TransformerEncoder with no positional encoding added and no [CLS]/ordering signal. Self-attention is permutation-equivariant, so without positional encoding the model is invariant to the order of IMU samples in the window — it literally cannot tell t=0 from t=99.
