pitfalls: QUATERNION CONVENTION MISMATCH is the dominant bug: scalar-first [w,x,y,z] (Eigen, ahrs lib, Madgwick, Brossard) vs scalar-last [x,y,z,w] (SciPy Rotation, ROS tf). The exact Omega(w) entries and Hamilton-product order depend on it. Mixing libraries silently rotates the wrong way / by the wrong axis. Pin one convention, assert it, and unit-test every library boundary.

HAMILTON vs JPL multiplication convention (ij=k vs ij=-k) and active vs passive rotation: a propagator copied from a JPL-convention paper (e.g. Trawny) into a Hamilton-convention codebase will be subtly wrong (sign flips in Omega, transposed rotation). Don't mix sources without checking the convention each one uses.

Forward-Euler (first-order) integration q_{k+1}=(I+(dt/2)Omega(w))q_k does NOT preserve unit norm and drifts for large |w|*dt; forgetting to renormalize, or using Euler where the closed-form is needed, degrades long open-loop dead reckoning. The closed-form exponential is exact for constant w over dt — prefer it.

Defining the Brossard loss on per-sample gyro error requires 200 Hz ground-truth rate that mocap cannot provide (mocap is 20-120 Hz) — the whole point of the integrated-increment loss (Eq.8-10) is to avoid this. Re-deriving a naive per-sample MSE loss reintroduces the problem the paper solved.

Setting the loss window j too large (e.g. whole-trajectory orientation error R^T R_hat) overfits to specific training trajectory patterns; too small reintroduces the high-frequency-ground-truth problem. The paper's L_16 + L_32 (12.5 Hz / 6.25 Hz error rates) is a deliberate sweet spot.

ReLU activation overfits sharp gyro corrections — the paper specifically uses GELU (smooth) and reports ReLU is worse; dropping batchnorm hurts training speed and accuracy. An RNN/LSTM substitute gives ~40% more ROE. Don't 'modernize' the tiny CNN into a heavy transformer/RNN without re-checking — ~77k params is a feature.

IMU/ground-truth TIME MISALIGNMENT makes the network learn a spurious time delay instead of denoising; non-constant sampling time corrupts the integration. Resample smartphone IMU to a clean fixed 200 Hz grid and tightly synchronize with ground truth before training.

Omitting accelerometer from the network input costs ~50% ROE (ablation) even though attitude is integrated open-loop from gyro only — accel input carries angular-rate information via slow-velocity assumption (Eq.7). Don't feed gyro alone.

Magnetometer on smartphones is heavily perturbed indoors (ferrous structures, electronics); naive MARG Madgwick / mag-update EKF can corrupt heading worse than gyro drift. Gate, calibrate (hard/soft-iron), or down-weight magnetic correction for indoor pedestrian use.

AOE is highly sensitive to WHERE in the sequence error occurs and to the t=0 alignment; using AOE alone to rank odometry methods is misleading — report ROE (fixed travelled-distance sub-windows, median/percentiles) as the primary metric, as the paper recommends.

Naive 4-quaternion EKF has a singular/over-parameterized 4-DoF covariance for a 3-DoF rotation, forcing fragile renormalization hacks; use the error-state Multiplicative EKF (MEKF) instead. Also: gyro is a PREDICT input (process noise), NOT a measurement — modeling it as an observation is a classic setup error.

C_w in Brossard is a STATIC learned 3x3 (axis-misalignment + scale) initialized to identity, while the bias is absorbed into the time-varying network output c_hat; conflating them (e.g. making C_w time-varying or learning an explicit bias state) departs from the published, well-behaved setup and the time-varying/multi-IMU case is explicitly left as future work.

research.topic: Quaternion / rotation loss functions for learning orientation (SO(3) geodesic, chordal/Frobenius, quaternion double-cover losses) for neural inertial navigation from smartphone IMU
key_techniques: GEODESIC (angular) DISTANCE on SO(3): d_geo(R1,R2) = arccos((tr(R1 R2^T) - 1) / 2), range [0, pi]. This is the angle of the relative rotation R1 R2^T and is the 'true' Riemannian distance on SO(3). It is the canonical EVALUATION metric (report mean/RMSE of this angle in degrees). Equivalent quaternion form: theta = 2*arccos(|<q1,q2>|).

LOG-MAP geodesic loss: d_log(R1,R2) = || log(R1 R2^T) ||, where log(.) is the SO(3) matrix logarithm mapping a rotation to its so(3) skew/axis-angle vector (norm = rotation angle). Equivalent to the geodesic angle. This is exactly the form Brossard et al. (gyro-denoising, RAL 2020) use: L_j = sum_i rho( log( dR_{i,i+j} dR_hat^T_{i,i+j} ) ) with rho = Huber loss (param 0.005), summed over multiple integration horizons (L = L16 + L32).

CHORDAL / FROBENIUS distance (matrices): d_chord(R1,R2) = ||R1 - R2||_F, range [0, 2*sqrt(2)]. Equivalent up-to-constant form ||I - R1 R2^T||_F. Its SQUARE, d_chord^2 = ||vec(R1 - R2)||^2 = sum of squared elementwise differences, is a plain MSE on the 9 matrix entries. Related to the geodesic angle by ||R1-R2||_F = 2*sqrt(2)*sin(theta/2). Smooth, convex-friendly, NO arccos -> no gradient singularity. This is the loss the 'Hitchhiker's guide to SO(3)' recommends paired with R9+SVD orthogonalization.

QUATERNION distance-picking I: d_qI = min(||q1 - q2||, ||q1 + q2||), range [0, sqrt(2)]. The min over (q, -q) resolves the double cover. Smooth almost everywhere; a plain L2 on quaternion coords with antipodal selection. Common simple regression loss (no arccos).

QUATERNION distance-picking II (cosine): d_qII = 1 - |<q1,q2>|, range [0, 1]. Uses absolute value of the quaternion inner product to handle q ~ -q. Monotonic in the rotation angle (1 - |cos(theta/2)|) but NOT the angle itself. Smooth, bounded gradient -> numerically the safest quaternion loss. RIANN cites prior work that replaces arccos with this '1 - a' linear-in-cosine term precisely to kill the gradient blowup.

QUATERNION angular (geodesic) loss: e_alpha = 2*arccos(|<q1,q2>|) (full attitude) or, for IMU attitude-only error, RIANN's e_alpha = 2*arccos(sqrt(w^2 + z^2)) on the error quaternion to isolate inclination from heading. This equals the geodesic angle but inherits the arccos gradient singularity at coincidence.

DOUBLE COVER (q ~ -q): unit quaternions are a 2-to-1 (double) cover of SO(3); q and -q encode the identical rotation. Any quaternion loss MUST be invariant to sign, achieved via |<q1,q2>| (absolute inner product) or min(||q1-q2||,||q1+q2||). Naive ||q1-q2||^2 without sign handling penalizes the correct rotation and gives the wrong gradient.

NETWORK OUTPUT TARGETS used in practice: (a) gyro/orientation INCREMENTS integrated over a window then compared via SO(3) log loss (Brossard) - avoids needing ground-truth at full IMU rate and is invariant to global rotation; (b) absolute unit quaternion with post-hoc normalization (OriNet, RIANN); (c) 6D continuous representation (Zhou et al., CVPR 2019, two columns of R + Gram-Schmidt) or 9D + SVD orthogonalization, which are CONTINUOUS maps from SO(3) and learn far better than 3D/4D (quaternion/Euler) targets.
concrete_recommendations: For the EVALUATION metric, always report the geodesic angle in degrees: theta = arccos((tr(R_pred R_gt^T)-1)/2) = 2*arccos(|<q_pred,q_gt>|). Report mean and RMSE over the trajectory. For IMU attitude where heading is unobservable without magnetometer, report the inclination-only error e_alpha = 2*arccos(sqrt(w^2+z^2)) of the error quaternion (RIANN) so heading drift does not pollute the attitude metric.

For the TRAINING loss, prefer a smooth surrogate that avoids arccos: either (a) chordal/Frobenius squared d_chord^2 = ||R_pred - R_gt||_F^2 on a properly orthogonalized matrix output (best paired with 6D-GSO or 9D-SVD), or (b) the quaternion cosine loss L = 1 - |<q_pred,q_gt>| (or 1 - <.>^2). Both have bounded gradients everywhere and are monotonic in the rotation angle.

If you DO want a geodesic/log-map loss (e.g. Brossard-style increment loss L = sum rho(||log(dR dR_hat^T)||) with Huber rho), implement it in float64 for the angle computation and CLAMP the arccos / trace argument to [-1+eps, 1-eps] (e.g. eps ~ 1e-6 .. 1e-7). The arccos derivative is -1/sqrt(1-a^2) -> -infinity as a->1, so without clamping you get NaN/Inf gradients exactly when the prediction is correct. RIANN's fix: 64-bit precision + cut values too close to 1.
Always make quaternion losses sign-invariant: use |<q1,q2>| or min(||q1-q2||,||q1+q2||). Never use raw ||q1-q2||^2 without antipodal selection or you train against the double cover.

Do NOT regress raw quaternions or Euler angles as the network's geometric output if accuracy matters: they are discontinuous as maps from SO(3) (Zhou et al. 2019), leaving a residual tail of ~180-degree errors that no loss choice removes. Output 6D (two columns + Gram-Schmidt) or 9D+SVD and convert to quaternion only for the loss/metric. For IMU work where motions stay near a hemisphere, a half-space-mapped quaternion can be acceptable but is strictly inferior.

Use the Brossard formulation when ground truth is only available at lower rate than the IMU (e.g. mocap at 20-120 Hz vs IMU at 200 Hz): supervise integrated relative increments dR_{i,i+j} over windows (j around 16 and 32 -> ~12 Hz and ~6 Hz) rather than per-sample gyro residuals or the global orientation error. Multi-horizon (L16 + L32) plus Huber gives robustness to mocap outliers and avoids overfitting to specific trajectory patterns; the increment loss is also invariant to a global left rotation, matching IMU symmetry.

Add a small unit-norm regularizer (||q||_2 - 1)^2 or normalize before computing the loss when outputting raw quaternions; equivalently use SVD/GSO so the orthogonalization is built in and no norm penalty is needed.

Geodesic vs chordal in practice: they induce the same global minimum and are boundedly equivalent (sin(theta/2) vs theta), so the choice is about gradients, not correctness. Chordal/cosine = smoother, no singularity, faster early convergence; geodesic = exactly the metric you report but needs clamping. A common robust recipe is to train with chordal/cosine (or Huber-on-log) and evaluate with geodesic degrees.

Defines six rotation distance functions Phi1..Phi6 (Euler-angle Euclidean; Phi2 Frobenius/chordal ||R1-R2||_F in [0,2sqrt2]; Phi3 geodesic arccos((tr(R1R2^T)-1)/2) in [0,pi]; Phi4 min(||q1-q2||,||q1+q2||) in [0,sqrt2]; Phi5 arccos(|<q1,q2>|) in [0,pi/2]; Phi6 1-|<q1,q2>| in [0,1]). citations.title: Denoising IMU Gyroscopes with Deep Learning for Open-Loop Attitude Estimation (Brossard, Barrau, Bonnabel)
citations.note: IEEE RA-L. Network = dilated CNN outputting gyro correction increments at 200 Hz. Loss based on integrated relative increments: dR_{i,i+j}=R_i^T R_{i+j}, L_j = sum_i rho(log(dR_{i,i+j} dR_hat^T_{i,i+j})), rho=Huber(0.005), log=SO(3) logarithm; final L=L16+L32. Invariant to global left rotation; multi-horizon avoids overfitting vs supervising the overall orientation error. Authors report no measurable difference between rotation-matrix and quaternion loss implementations.

citations.title: RIANN - A Robust Neural Network Outperforms Attitude Estimation Filters (Weber, Gühmann, Seel)
citations.note: AI 2(3):28. GRU network on accel+gyro outputting unit quaternions. Metric/loss e_alpha(tk)=2*arccos(sqrt(w^2+z^2)) on the error quaternion (inclination only), eMSE = mean of e_alpha^2. Explicitly states the arccos gradient grows unbounded as argument->1 (d arccos(a)/da = -1/sqrt(1-a^2) -> -inf). Two fixes discussed: prior work [their conference paper] replaces arccos by linear 1-a (loses metric exactness); RIANN instead uses float64 + clamps values too close to 1 for a numerically stable direct metric.

citations.title: Learning with 3D rotations, a hitchhiker's guide to SO(3) (Geist, Frey, Zhou et al.)
citations.note: Survey of rotation representations and losses for learning. Restates geodesic arccos((trR1R2^T-1)/2), chordal ||R1-R2||_F, quaternion 1-|<q1,q2>| and min(||q1-q2||,||q1+q2||). Recommends R9+SVD (or R6+GSO) with squared chordal/Frobenius MSE; argues changing the loss does not fix the double-cover discontinuity of low-dim (quaternion/Euler) targets - you must move to continuous high-dim representations.

citations.title: On the Continuity of Rotation Representations in Neural Networks (Zhou, Barnes, Lu, Yang, Li)
citations.note: CVPR 2019. Proves all SO(3) representations in <=4 real dimensions (quaternions, Euler, axis-angle) are discontinuous, hurting NN learning; introduces continuous 6D (two matrix columns + Gram-Schmidt) and 5D representations. Empirically 6D/5D converge faster with errors <2 deg while quaternion/Euler leave a tail up to 180 deg. Justifies choosing the output target, not just the loss.

citations.title: OriNet: Robust 3-D Orientation Estimation With a Single Particular IMU (Esfahani et al.)
citations.note: IEEE RA-L. First deep (LSTM) framework estimating full 3D orientation as a quaternion from a single IMU; uses a quaternion-based loss. Primary inertial-orientation reference using quaternion regression.

pitfalls: ARCCOS GRADIENT BLOWUP / NaN: d/da arccos(a) = -1/sqrt(1-a^2) diverges to -infinity as a -> 1 (i.e. exactly when the prediction is correct). A geodesic loss arccos((tr-1)/2) or 2*arccos(|<q1,q2>|) therefore produces NaN/Inf gradients near the optimum and destabilizes training. Mitigate with float64 + clamp the arccos argument to [-1+eps, 1-eps] (RIANN), or replace arccos by the linear-in-cosine surrogate 1-a (loses exact-angle interpretation).

FORGETTING DOUBLE COVER: training ||q_pred - q_gt||^2 without sign handling penalizes a perfectly correct rotation whenever the network outputs -q_gt, injecting a wrong gradient. Always use |<.>| or min(||q1-q2||,||q1+q2||).

ASSUMING A BETTER LOSS FIXES DISCONTINUITY: with a 3D/4D output target (quaternion, Euler, axis-angle) the map from SO(3) is inherently discontinuous; no loss removes the residual ~180-degree error tail. The fix is the representation (6D-GSO / 9D-SVD), not the loss (Hitchhiker's guide; Zhou et al.).

CONFUSING METRIC WITH SURROGATE: chordal/cosine distances are monotonic in the angle but are NOT the angle (||R1-R2||_F = 2sqrt2 sin(theta/2); 1-|<q1,q2>| = 1-|cos(theta/2)|). Use the geodesic angle (degrees) for reporting; using chordal numbers as if they were degrees misstates accuracy.
NON-UNIT QUATERNIONS: regressing raw 4-vectors without normalization (or without SVD/GSO) drifts off the unit sphere, making <q1,q2> not a valid cosine; normalize before the loss or add (||q||-1)^2.

SUPERVISING AT THE WRONG RATE/SCOPE: requiring per-sample gyro ground truth at full 200 Hz is infeasible (mocap is 20-120 Hz), and supervising the global orientation error R^T R_hat overfits to training trajectories. Brossard's integrated-increment loss over modest horizons (j~16,32) is the practical middle ground.
MISSING-GT GAPS: optical mocap has occlusion gaps; integrating/interpolating across them corrupts the target. Mask those intervals out of the loss/minibatch (RIANN) rather than filling them.

DASTANCE-PICKING II IS NOT A TRUE ANGLE-LINEAR LOSS: 1-|<q1,q2>| flattens (gradient -> 0) only at theta=0 and theta=pi but is fine in between; combined with double cover it is well behaved, yet its small-angle curvature differs from the geodesic, so do not mix it with degree-based early-stopping thresholds without conversion.

research.topic: Practical training methodology for neural-network IMU sequence regression (pedestrian inertial odometry from smartphone IMU at ~200 Hz): windowing, frame/output target choice, train-only normalization, evaluation protocol (ATE/RTE), target-leakage avoidance, and IMU augmentation.
key_techniques: Output target = local 2D velocity or short-horizon displacement, NOT absolute position. RoNIN regresses a 2D horizontal velocity v = (P_i - P_{i-w})/dt with w=200 frames (1 s); TLIO regresses a 3D displacement vector d = position difference between two instants. The network never sees or outputs absolute position; trajectory is obtained by integrating/concatenating local outputs at inference. This is what makes the problem learnable and drift-bounded.

Heading-agnostic / gravity-aligned coordinate frame for BOTH inputs and outputs. RoNIN defines a Heading-Agnostic Coordinate Frame (HACF) = any frame whose Z axis is aligned with gravity; raw accel+gyro are rotated into this frame via device orientation quaternions before being fed to the net, and the 2D velocity target is expressed in the same horizontal plane. TLIO uses a gravity-aligned local frame (gravity pointing down). Expressing in a gravity-aligned frame removes the arbitrary device yaw/attitude and is the single biggest robustness lever.

Sequence-to-one (window -> single vector) is the dominant, simplest formulation: a fixed window of IMU samples maps to one velocity/displacement vector (RoNIN ResNet, TLIO). RoNIN also offers sequence-to-sequence (LSTM/TCN) variants that emit a velocity per step over the unrolled window with a 'latent/strided velocity loss'. For a clean reimplementation, start with sequence-to-one + 1D ResNet.

Window length & stride (concrete, at 200 Hz): RoNIN ResNet uses window_size=200 samples (1 s); training stride/step_size=10 samples (heavy overlap, ~95%); the sequence-to-sequence config uses window_size=400 (2 s), step_size=100. TLIO uses a 1 s (200-sample) window over 6 channels. Cross-dataset survey (Keller et al. 2025) lists per-dataset window/stride: RoNIN 200/10, RIDI 200/100, EuRoC 200/100, QuadNet 120/60. Larger windows = more context but more averaging/latency; small training stride = more samples + augmentation effect.

6-channel input (3-axis accelerometer + 3-axis gyroscope), magnetometer typically NOT used by the regressor (it's noisy/disturbed indoors and orientation is handled via the gravity-aligned frame). RoNIN calibrates first: subtract gyro bias, apply accel scale+bias, then rotate both into the global gravity-aligned frame and concatenate to an N x 6 tensor.

Loss = MSE on the velocity/displacement vector (RoNIN strided velocity loss = MSE between net output at frame i and P_i - P_{i-200}). TLIO uses two-stage training: 10 epochs plain MSE, then 10 epochs Gaussian maximum-likelihood (NLL) that also regresses a diagonal covariance: L_ML = (1/n) sum [ 0.5 log det(Sigma_i) + 0.5 ||d_i - d_hat_i||^2_{Sigma_i} ], Sigma = diag(exp(2u)). MSE is a strong, hard-to-beat baseline; L1/Huber/LogCosh give within +/-1% (Keller et al. 2025).

IMU-specific augmentation, in order of impact (Keller et al. 2025; TLIO): (1) RANDOM HORIZONTAL/YAW ROTATION about gravity is the dominant augmentation (RoNIN applies random HACF yaw each sample; gives ~7% average gain and yaw-invariance). (2) Additive Gaussian NOISE on accel/gyro (~6% gain; e.g. ~0.1 m/s^2 accel, ~0.001 rad/s gyro). (3) Additive BIAS perturbation (smaller, ~2% gain). TLIO uses accel bias ~U(+/-0.2 m/s^2), gyro bias ~U(+/-0.05 rad/s), and gravity-direction tilt of [0,5] degrees about a random horizontal axis.

Per-trajectory evaluation: compute ATE and RTE PER recording, then AVERAGE (and report std/CDF) across all test recordings. Critically, hold out ENTIRE subjects/recordings for test (RoNIN: 100 subjects split into seen group 1 = train/val/test-seen and unseen group 2 = generalization test), never split windows from the same trajectory across train and test.
concrete_recommendations: Pick the target as a LOCAL quantity expressed in a gravity-aligned frame. Recommended default: sequence-to-one 1D ResNet-18 (input N x 6) that regresses the 2D horizontal velocity v = (p_{t} - p_{t-w}) / (w/fs), with w=200, fs=200 Hz (1 s window). Integrate v over time at inference to get the trajectory. This is RoNIN ResNet and is the most reproducible baseline.

Rotate accel+gyro into the gravity-aligned frame BEFORE the network using an orientation estimate. At train time RoNIN/TLIO use the ground-truth/VIO orientation; this is a deliberate, acceptable use of GT (orientation only, NOT position/velocity). To prevent the model overfitting to perfect orientation, add gravity-tilt augmentation ([0,5] deg about a random horizontal axis) so it tolerates the noisier orientation available at runtime. Never feed ground-truth position, velocity, or heading as a network INPUT feature.

Set window=200 samples (1 s) and training stride=10 samples (RoNIN default) for dense overlapping windows; this both maximizes training samples and acts as implicit augmentation. Use a non-overlapping or stride=window evaluation so each test segment is scored once. At 200 Hz a 1 s window balances motion context vs latency; only enlarge to 2 s (window=400) if moving to an LSTM/TCN sequence-to-sequence variant.

Default loss = MSE on the velocity/displacement vector. Do NOT switch to L1/Huber expecting gains (within +/-1% in the cross-dataset study). If you also want calibrated uncertainty for downstream EKF fusion (TLIO-style), add a diagonal-covariance head and train in two stages: MSE first, then Gaussian NLL.

Be deliberate about per-channel normalization. The literature is split: (a) general ML hygiene says fit any StandardScaler mean/std on the TRAIN split ONLY and reuse those stats on val/test to avoid leakage; (b) RoNIN/TLIO do NOT z-score the rotated IMU channels at all, and Keller et al. (2025) found z-score/robust normalization DEGRADED neural inertial regression badly (avg -308% to -907%). Recommendation: default to NO feature normalization beyond sensor calibration + gravity-frame rotation; if you must normalize, compute mean/std on train only and never on the full dataset.

Apply IMU augmentation every batch, prioritizing: random yaw rotation about gravity (always), then additive Gaussian noise (~0.1 m/s^2 accel, ~0.001 rad/s gyro), then small constant bias offsets (accel ~U(+/-0.2 m/s^2), gyro ~U(+/-0.05 rad/s)), then gravity-tilt [0,5] deg. Skip magnetometer entirely for the regressor.

Evaluation protocol: report ATE and RTE in meters, computed PER trajectory then averaged over all test recordings (also report median/std or a CDF). ATE = RMSE between estimated and ground-truth positions over the whole aligned trajectory. RTE = average RMSE of position error over fixed-length sub-windows; USE A 1-MINUTE WINDOW (RoNIN's convention). Concretely: slide a 60 s (12000-sample at 200 Hz) window, for each compute the position-difference error of the estimate vs GT over that window, RMSE within the window, then average over windows and over recordings.

Split by SUBJECT/recording, not by window. Hold out entire unseen subjects for the main generalization number (RoNIN group 2 of 15/100 subjects) plus a seen-subject test set. This is the only honest way to measure generalization and prevents the same trajectory leaking into both train and test via overlapping windows.

citations.title: TLIO: Tight Learned Inertial Odometry (Liu et al.; RA-L/IROS 2020)
citations.note: Primary source. Regresses 3D displacement d + diagonal covariance in a gravity-aligned local frame; 1 s / 200-sample window over 6 channels; 1D ResNet-18; two-stage training: 10 epochs MSE then 10 epochs Gaussian NLL L_ML=mean[0.5 log det(Sigma)+0.5||d-d_hat||^2_Sigma], Sigma=diag(exp(2u)); augmentation: random horizontal (yaw) rotation, accel bias U(+/-0.2 m/s^2), gyro bias U(+/-0.05 rad/s), gravity tilt [0,5] deg; Adam lr=1e-4, dropout 0.5. Training rotates by GT orientation (orientation only); perturbations bridge to noisier runtime orientation.

citations.title: Enhancement of Neural Inertial Regression Networks: A Data-Driven Perspective (Keller, Klein et al.)
citations.note: Cross-dataset study. Rotation aug ~30 deg (pi/6) -> +7% avg; noise aug -> +6% (7/8 datasets); bias aug -> +2% (4/8); accel 0.1 m/s^2, gyro 0.001 rad/s for bias/noise. Per-dataset window/stride: RoNIN 200/10, RIDI 200/100, EuRoC 200/100, QuadNet 120/60, MoRPI 360/60, DoorINet 20/20. KEY: normalization (standard/robust z-score) DEGRADED results (avg -308% / -907%) -> 'the actual inertial measurement should not be normalized'. L1/Huber/LogCosh within +/-1% of MSE.

citations.title: Deep Learning for Inertial Positioning: A Survey (Chen, Pan)
citations.note: ATE = average RMSE between actual and predicted locations over the entire trajectory; RTE = average RMSE within a specified time interval. Confirms RIDI/RoNIN use heading-agnostic gravity-aligned frame, TLIO gravity-aligned frame, others body frame.

citations.title: RIDI: Robust IMU Double Integration (Yan, Shan, Furukawa; ECCV 2018)
citations.note: Earlier velocity-regression approach: regress a 2D velocity from accel+gyro history, correct low-freq accel errors so integration matches regressed velocity, then double-integrate. Predecessor framing to RoNIN's direct velocity regression.

citations.title: How to Avoid Data Leakage When Performing Data Preparation (Brownlee, MachineLearningMastery)
citations.note: General principle: fit scalers (mean/std) on TRAIN split only, then apply to val/test; fitting on the full dataset before splitting leaks test statistics and inflates measured performance.

pitfalls: TARGET LEAKAGE via the input frame: rotating IMU into a gravity-aligned frame requires an orientation estimate. Using ground-truth ORIENTATION at train time is standard and acceptable (RoNIN/TLIO), but it is a hidden dependency on GT. If you instead leak ground-truth POSITION/VELOCITY/HEADING as an input feature, the model collapses to copying it and fails at inference. Keep only orientation, and add gravity-tilt augmentation so the model survives the noisier runtime orientation.

NORMALIZATION LEAKAGE: computing per-channel mean/std (or min/max) over the full dataset before the train/test split lets test statistics bleed into training and inflates reported accuracy. Always fit scalers on train only. Worse for this domain: z-scoring the IMU at all tends to HURT neural inertial regression (Keller et al. 2025 found large degradations), because absolute accel/gyro magnitudes carry the motion signal - prefer raw (calibrated, gravity-rotated) channels.

WINDOW LEAKAGE across splits: with a small stride (e.g. 10 samples), adjacent windows are ~95% identical. If you shuffle windows then split, near-duplicate windows land in both train and test, giving optimistic numbers. Split by subject/recording, generate windows within each split, never across.

Reporting a single global ATE/RTE over concatenated trajectories instead of per-trajectory-then-averaged hides per-recording variance and is incomparable to the literature. Always compute per recording and average (report std or CDF).

Ambiguous RTE definition: RTE is meaningless without stating the time window. RoNIN uses 1 minute. Report the window explicitly (e.g. RTE@60s); comparing an RTE@1min against someone's RTE@10s is invalid.
Predicting absolute position directly (sequence -> full trajectory) makes the model memorize venue geometry and generalize terribly; regress LOCAL velocity/displacement and integrate instead.

Including magnetometer in the regressor: indoor magnetic disturbance makes it unreliable; most SOTA pedestrian regressors (RoNIN/TLIO) use only the 6-channel accel+gyro and handle heading via the gravity-aligned frame, not the magnetometer.

Over-large windows add latency and average out fast motion (turns), inflating RTE on dynamic segments; over-small windows lose the integration context needed to estimate velocity. 1 s (200 samples) at 200 Hz is the validated sweet spot.

Forgetting yaw-rotation augmentation: without random rotation about gravity, the network overfits to the training subjects' habitual headings/device orientations and fails to generalize - it is the highest-impact augmentation (~7%), so omitting it is a major regression.

research.topic: 1D-CNN/ResNet and Transformer-encoder architectures for IMU time-series regression (pedestrian inertial odometry from 6-axis IMU windows)
key_techniques: 1D ResNet-18 (channel-first conv1d) is the de-facto backbone for IMU window regression. RoNIN and TLIO both use it. Input is a [B, C=6, L] tensor (channel-first: 3-axis accel + 3-axis gyro stacked as channels, time as the conv axis), NOT [B, L, C]. The whole standard ResNet-18 2D recipe maps to 1D by swapping Conv2d/BatchNorm2d/MaxPool2d -> Conv1d/BatchNorm1d/MaxPool1d.

RoNIN ResNet1D exact structure (from official source/model_resnet1d.py): input head Conv1d(6, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3) -> BatchNorm1d -> ReLU -> MaxPool1d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1); then 4 stages with group_sizes=[2,2,2,2] BasicBlock1D and channel widths [64,128,256,512] (base_plane=64, planes = base_plane*2**i); each BasicBlock1D = two Conv1d(kernel_size=k, padding=k//2) + BN + ReLU with identity/projection skip; head = AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) (global average pooling over time) -> Linear(512, num_outputs). num_inputs=6, num_outputs=2.

Global average pooling over the time axis (AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1)) is the standard way the CNN reduces a variable/fixed-length window to a single regression vector. This preserves translation tolerance and gives a length-robust head. (The RoNIN paper text mentions a '512-unit FC'; the released code actually uses GlobAvgOutputModule = AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) then Linear(512->2). Trust the code.)

Output target and frame convention (RoNIN): regress a 2D velocity vector in a Heading-Agnostic Coordinate Frame (HACF) - any frame whose Z axis is gravity-aligned. Train-time augmentation applies random yaw (horizontal-plane) rotations to input and target together so the net is heading-invariant. Loss = MSE between the 2D output and (P_i - P_{i-200})/dt-style strided position difference (the 'strided velocity loss'). Trajectory = integrate predicted velocities. TLIO instead regresses a 3D relative displacement plus a diagonal covariance in a gravity-aligned frame, trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood loss, then fuses into a stochastic-cloning EKF.

Window/sampling conventions at 200Hz: RoNIN/TLIO/CTIN use a 200-sample window (= 1 s at 200Hz) of 6 channels -> [6, 200] tensor. At test time RoNIN predicts every 5 frames (stride 5) and integrates. Magnetometer is recorded but NOT fed to the regression net in RoNIN/TLIO (orientation-dependent, hard to use raw); accel+gyro = 6 channels is the standard input.

Transformer-encoder for fixed-length IMU windows - canonical pattern (Zerveas et al. 'A Transformer-based Framework for Multivariate Time Series', TST): (a) per-timestep input projection via a single nn.Linear(n_channels -> d_model) applied at every time step (treats each timestep's 6-vector as a token; scale by sqrt(d_model)); (b) ADD a positional encoding (fixed sinusoidal or learnable) - mandatory because self-attention is permutation-invariant; (c) stack of TransformerEncoderLayer (multi-head self-attention + FFN). TST defaults: d_model=128, n_heads=8-16 (default 16), num_layers=3, dim_feedforward=256-512, dropout~0.1.

Reducing the encoder sequence [L, d_model] to a single regression output - three valid options: (1) mean-pool over time then Linear(d_model -> out) [robust, length-agnostic, recommended default for IMU]; (2) prepend a learnable CLS token and read its final embedding -> Linear(d_model -> out) [BERT-style]; (3) flatten all timesteps and Linear(d_model*L -> out) [what TST actually does for regression; only valid for FIXED L, large param count]. For fixed L=200 IMU windows, mean-pool or CLS are cleaner and generalize better than flatten.

CTIN (AAAI 2022, 'Robust Contextual Transformer Network for Inertial Navigation') - a ResNet+Transformer hybrid tuned for this exact task: input N=200 x 6 at 200Hz; a ResNet-18-style spatial encoder where spatial conv is augmented with local self-attention and a global self-attention module (Nx=1 encoder layer); a Transformer DECODER with Nx=4 layers fuses temporal context (temporal embedding = 1-layer BiLSTM + a learned/trainable positional encoding); two MLP heads regress 2D velocity AND its 2x2 covariance; multi-task loss = integral velocity loss (position + cumulative-error terms) + covariance negative-log-likelihood + homoscedastic-uncertainty weighting (1/(2 sigma_v^2) L_v + 1/(2 sigma_c^2) L_c + log sigma_v sigma_c, sigmas learned per Kendall multi-task uncertainty). Evaluated on RIDI, OxIOD, RoNIN, IDOL.

iMoT (AAAI 2025) uses an iTransformer-style 'variate token' scheme: instead of one token per timestep, the ENTIRE time series of each variate (channel) becomes a token of dimension T (=window length, 100 or 200 to match the Hz). Encoder N=2, decoder M=2, with an Adaptive Positional Encoding (sinusoidal base scaled by learned per-modality factors) and a learned set of P=128 'query motion particles' in the decoder; final velocity = score-weighted combination of particle predictions; loss = MSE on velocity (+ optional entropy regularizer on particle scores).

Standard evaluation metrics for trajectory regression: ATE (Absolute Trajectory Error) = RMSE between estimated and ground-truth positions over the whole trajectory after integration; RTE (Relative Trajectory Error) = average RMSE over a fixed time window (RoNIN uses 1 minute). Report both; ATE rewards low long-horizon drift, RTE measures local accuracy. Also report per-window velocity/displacement MSE for the direct regression target.
concrete_recommendations: Backbone default: implement a 1D ResNet-18 channel-first. Module signature ResNet1D(in_channels=6, num_outputs=2, block=BasicBlock1D, layers=[2,2,2,2], base_channels=64). Input head: Conv1d(6,64,kernel_size=7,stride=2,padding=3) + BatchNorm1d(64) + ReLU + MaxPool1d(3,stride=2,padding=1). Stages widths [64,128,256,512], first block of stages 2-4 strides 2 with a 1x1 conv projection on the skip. Head: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) -> flatten -> nn.Linear(512, num_outputs). This is a faithful, minimal RoNIN-equivalent.

Feed the IMU window as a [batch, 6, 200] tensor (channel-first). Do NOT transpose to [batch, 200, 6] for conv1d - conv1d convolves over the LAST dim, so time must be last and the 6 sensor axes must be the channel dim. Normalize each channel (per-channel mean/std from train set); accel and gyro have very different scales.

Pick the regression target and frame deliberately and document it: regress 2D (or 3D) velocity/displacement in a gravity-aligned, heading-agnostic frame, integrate to get trajectory. Add yaw-rotation data augmentation that rotates input IMU and target velocity together so the network is heading-invariant (this is RoNIN's key trick for in-the-wild robustness). Train the CNN with plain MSE on the velocity/displacement target; integrate at inference (stride ~5 frames).

Transformer encoder reference config for ~6-channel, length-200 IMU windows: d_model=128, nhead=8, num_layers=4 (try 2-6), dim_feedforward=256 (2x-4x d_model), dropout=0.1, GELU activation, batch_first=True, norm_first=True (pre-LN trains more stably). Input projection = nn.Linear(6, 128) applied per timestep. Add sinusoidal positional encoding sized [200,128]. This is comparable param-count to ResNet-18-1D and a fair A/B baseline.

For the transformer regression head, default to mean-pooling over the time dimension (output.mean(dim=1)) followed by a small MLP/Linear to the 2-D target; offer a CLS-token variant (prepend one learnable [1,1,d_model] token, slice its output) behind a flag. Avoid the flatten-all-timesteps head unless you specifically want to reproduce Zerveas TST; it ties the model to fixed L=200 and blows up parameters (200*128 -> out).

Always ADD positional encoding before the encoder layers. Self-attention is permutation-invariant; without PE the transformer cannot use temporal order and will silently underperform (it effectively becomes a set/bag-of-timesteps model). Verify by an ablation: shuffling the time axis should change a correct model's output - if it doesn't, your PE is missing or not being added.

Set nhead >= 4 (8 is a safe default) and ensure d_model is divisible by nhead. nhead=1 collapses multi-head attention to a single head and loses the main benefit (multiple representation subspaces); it is a common silent misconfiguration. With d_model=128, nhead=8 gives head_dim=16, a reasonable per-head width.

If you want a stronger model than either pure baseline, replicate the CTIN recipe: ResNet-1D spatial front-end -> sinusoidal/learned PE -> a few TransformerEncoder layers (CTIN uses 1 'spatial' encoder + 4 decoder layers) -> dual MLP heads predicting velocity AND a (log-)variance, trained with Gaussian NLL + Kendall homoscedastic multi-task weighting. The covariance head is what lets you fuse into an EKF later (TLIO-style).

Build the evaluation harness around ATE and RTE: integrate predicted velocities to a trajectory, compute ATE = RMSE of position error over the full track and RTE = RMSE over fixed 1-minute sub-windows; also log the raw per-window velocity MSE. Evaluate against RoNIN's released splits if possible so numbers are comparable to literature.

Keep an MLP-on-flattened-window as a deliberately-weak sanity baseline only (e.g. Linear(6*200 -> ...)). Expect it to be clearly worse than the CNN/transformer; if it is competitive, your CNN/transformer is mis-wired (bad normalization, missing PE, wrong tensor layout).

citations.note: Multi-head's main benefit is training stability vs equally-deep single-head; supports keeping nhead>=4-8 rather than nhead=1 in shallow encoders.

pitfalls: Wrong tensor layout for conv1d: feeding [batch, time, channels] instead of [batch, channels, time]. conv1d convolves over the last axis, so time MUST be last and the 6 sensor axes MUST be the channel dimension. Getting this backwards convolves across sensor axes and silently destroys the model.
nhead=1 in the transformer: collapses multi-head attention to a single head, losing the multiple-subspace benefit; also a frequent copy-paste default. Use nhead 4-8 and ensure d_model % nhead == 0.

Omitting positional encoding: self-attention is permutation-invariant, so without PE the transformer treats the window as an unordered set and cannot model temporal dynamics (velocity is inherently about temporal change). The failure is silent - it just trains to a worse plateau. Sanity check: shuffling timesteps should change the output.

Flattening the window into an MLP (Linear(6*200 -> ...)) as the actual model: destroys translation/temporal structure, explodes parameters, overfits, and is brittle to window-length changes. Fine as a weak baseline, wrong as the main architecture. The same critique applies to a transformer 'flatten-all-timesteps' head vs mean-pool/CLS for generalization.

Regressing in the raw device frame instead of a gravity-aligned, heading-agnostic frame (and skipping yaw augmentation): the network must then memorize device orientation, which wrecks in-the-wild generalization. RoNIN's HACF + random-yaw augmentation is the fix.

Feeding magnetometer raw into the regressor expecting free heading: magnetometer is orientation-dependent and indoor-distorted; RoNIN/TLIO deliberately use only accel+gyro (6ch). Adding mag naively often hurts.

Forgetting per-channel normalization: accelerometer (~m/s^2, includes gravity) and gyroscope (~rad/s) have very different scales; un-normalized inputs make the first conv/projection dominated by one modality.

Trusting paper prose over released code for the head: RoNIN's text says '512-unit FC' but the code uses global average pooling then Linear(512->2). Reimplementing the prose literally (a giant flatten+FC) gives a different, worse model.
Evaluating only per-window MSE and not integrating: low velocity MSE can still integrate to large drift. Always report ATE and RTE on integrated trajectories, not just the regression loss.

Post-LN + deep encoder without warmup can be unstable on small IMU datasets; prefer norm_first=True (pre-LN) and/or LR warmup. Also watch d_model too large for the dataset size - d_model=128, 2-4 layers is usually enough for length-200 6-channel windows; bigger transformers overfit these datasets where 1D-ResNet-18 is already strong.
